In Scotland,the divorce laws are more just to men, but there are many inequalities in the English statutes, which required to be removed. The law should be the same for the rich and the poor, and the same for both sexes, and it is not in either respect as it stands. To all intents and purposes divorce is open only to the rich. Every year there are thousands of women who obtain separation orders against drunken and dissolute husbands, on evidence that would entitle them to a divorce, but who have not the means to take their case to London, 'A here there is the only Court that can give them full relief. The effect of these orders is to prevent there-marriage of either party, and would seem to most people to produce more mischief than they check. Either there should be local divorce tribunals, in which the procedure is not necessarily costly, or else seisaration orders should be given the effect of dissolution of marriage after three or five years. Reform must, of course, proceed carefully, and with due regard to the danger of setting up one social evil for another, but if there is to he divorce at all, it shculd be the common right of the people, not the privilege of the rich, and there should not be one law for husbands, and another for wives. div.head: PILES FROM WET CLOTHING.
div.p: PILES FROM WET CLOTHING.
Distressing DiSanZ3 Curt-A 1.1,y Zam-Buk.

Piles frequently result from exposure t) wet and cold, and all those engaged in out-door occupations should read how Zarn-Buk has just completely cured a young worker. Mr. George A. Masc:n, 'a Thames vraterman and lighterman, of 14, Cwarloc-street, East Greenwich, London, S.E., said to a London reporter :—" Return- ing to work after a bad attack of rheumatism, I was struck down with bleedinr? piles. I was not very strong after the rheumatistrrleft me, and was scarcely fit to keep at my work all day in wet clothes. The consequence was that the piles became very bad, bleeding a great deal, and causing me endless misery. I could not sit down, and even when standing quite Still the irritation and burning from the inflamed skin were almost unbearable. Sleep was impossible, and naturally after my illness I soon got in a very weak state. _ _ _

" I did not neglect any advice offered, hat though I tried all kinds of medicines and ordinary ointments, it was only to be constantly disappointed. It seemed as though my complaint had taken too strong a hold on me to be effectually removed The bleeding and the pain and inflammation increased, and I was medically advised to undergo an operation. "It was quite by a happy chance that I was saved from this. My wife had been trying Zam-Buk for the children's bruises and cuts, and found it such a splendid healer that she persuaded me to try it too. Soon after commencing with Zam-Buk I expetienced a most sooth;ng sensation, such as I had never known since the piles first began. Perseverance was, of course, necessary, but by degrees the pain all went away,. Finally, the piles dried up completely, leaving me quite free from pain and worry. Once free of the piles I rapidly regained good health. "My wife and I also find Zam-Buk -splendid for chapped hands. In my work as a waterman, my hands are almost always wet and chap terribly in cold weather When I finish work I now dry my hands and arms thoroughly and then rub Zam-Buk over, the skin. This takes the burning sensation away, and heals the cracks and chaps. Zam-Buk is the greatest treasure in our home and we always keep a box handy."

PREVENTS qDIGESTION.
A HINT OF COMING FASUION.

From Vienna comes a hint of advanced fashions in tailor-Made costumes. These, will be on very modified Dircctoire lines, with coats that are cut long enough almost to reach the knee, sloped towards the back, with sleeves made very tight-fitting, and finished with little gauntlets; revers trimmed with buttons and edged with braid promise to be a distinguishing feature of the new coats. Skirts are cut on close, quiet, but by no means tube-like lines, while the favourite ma- terials for such costumes arc " Ilarquise " and plain Vienna cloth 3.

An authority states that the best test for cylinder oils Is to heat them in a current of air for one hour at the temperature corre- sponding to the steam pressure at which they are to work. The loss in weight should not exceed 0'& per cent.
NORMAL TEMPERATURE OF THE BODY.

Put to the test of the thermometer, it ap- pears that the normal temperature • of the body is almost invariable, regardless of lati- tude or season. Putting the bulb of the ther- mometer under the tongue of an Esquimau at the frozen north or of a man under the blazing sun of the tropics, we find that in each case, the body being in a state of health, the temperature is about the eame, the dif- ference not amounting to a degree. We may say absolutely that the average normal tem- perature of a human being is about 98.5 deg. Fahr., just as we may say that at sea level water boils at 212cleg. Fahr.

div.head: CIiEPE-DE-CHrIcE BLOUSE
div.p: CIiEPE-DE-CHrIcE BLOUSE

A blouse of almond - green crêpe-de-chine is sheNvn in our sketch. It is trimmed with bands of silk embroidery worked in shades of green, with a little gold thread worked in, on a cream net foundation. The whole of the bodice is arranged in pleats; the pleats being carried well over the shoulders, and repeated in the short sleeves. The neck is cut out in a small square, and finished with a band of the trimming. A second row of trimming forms a

larger square, and shews the pleats of the material between the two rows. The embroi- dery is carried over the shoulders and down the sleeves and finishes the edge, a second row being placed a little above it; the sleeves and corners of the yoke are adorned with green silk tassels, and the small guimpe and long cuffs are of finely - tucked net.

div.head: EDUCATED SERVANTS
div.p: EDUCATED SERVANTS

Someone was remarking to me the other day, writes "Lady Phyllis" in the B !Mandel., that even now, when women's professions have become so many and varied, domestic service has not yet been made honourable for the educated. Except in the case of children's nurses, no great public voice has arisen to greet the lady servant. Instead, the servant is supposed to be always of the working classes, more or less illiterate, and as the Board Schools go. gaily on even the working classes hold themselves "above " her func- tions. What is to happen? Some determined effort should be made to class domestic ser- vice as one of the professions for educated girls. It is an honourable occupation, • and one on which much of the comfort, ami- ability, and convenience of daily life depend. It is, moreover, pre-eminently suited to many girls of sound common sense and good educa- tion who have yet no great bent or talent, but are, almost by nature, quiet, capable, in- dustrious housewives. STRAIOtiT AND NARROW SKIRTS.

Straight and narrow skirts will be very fashionable as the summer advances. An effort will be made to introduce handsome trimmings at the hem, which will be in strik- ing contrast to the now popular straight up- and-down effects so becoming to the majority of women. Though the net sleeves are pro- mised an. immense vogue, says ,the Taller, long sleeves of soft satin will frequently be seen on the gowns fashioned of .voile, muslin, and other light materials suitable for sum- mer wear. A very charming gown of powder- blue voile had the sheath sleeves and ceinture of satin of the same shade, the clou of the whole being the waistcoat of. toile-de-Jouy outlined with black and surmounted with a guimpe of alternate rows of tucked net and lace.

div.head: WOMEN ELECTORS.
div.p: WOMEN ELECTORS.

A Local Government Board return shows that in Englanft there are 563,961 women and in Wales 41,945 qualified to vote in County Council elections; 259,827 in England and 6,035 in Wales qualified to vote for Borough Councils in county boroughs, and 131,421 in England and 5,903 in Wales qualified to vote for Borough Councils in non-county boroughs.

div.head: Cl.Ol'H COSTUME
div.p: Cl.Ol'H COSTUME

The costume depicted here is developed in indigo souple cloth, trimmed with black silk braid. The coat is semi-fitting, and has just a suspicion of the short - waisted effect. The sides of the coat are cut square at the ends, and are much longer than the fronts, which are cut with Mitred ends and outlined with Use braid. There is a line of braid over the

" shoulders, which is carried round the lower edge of the coat. The large hip-pockets- are ' outlined with braid, and adorned with large buttons, covered with black satin. The low- cut roll collar is faced with black satin, a handsome embroidered button being placed at the point of the revers. The sleeves are close- fitting, and trimmed at the top with little mitred tabs of braid. • The skirt is walking length, and is arranged in pleats, a trimming of black braid adorning the bottom of the skirt. TO-DAY'S RECIPE. CHERRY AND MACAROON PUDDING. Line a buttered mould with preserved cherries. Then spread a layer of milk-bread, finely sliced, at the bottom. Cover with a thick layer of crushed macaroons. Repeat the cherries, sliced bread, and macaroons alternately until the mould is full. On completing every triple layer a little brandy should be poured in, two wineglassfuis in all being used. Then beat up the yolk's and whites of four eggs together. Add to them a pint of milk, or preferably half a pint, each of cream and milk. Sweeten to taste, and stir in the rind of half a . lemon, grated. 'Pour the liquid over the pudding so that it moistens it vemy. anon flour a eic;rn, lay it over trio top, tie it down tightly, and boil the pudding for one hour. The mould mu,Et be kept the right side up, and- when ready the contents turned out and served with a sweet sauce made of cherry jaw, flavoured with a little sherry.

div.head: UPPER ATMOSPHERE.
div.p: THE UPPER ATMOSPHERE.

Samples of r.ir from the upper atmosphere have been collected by an investigator of its constituents in a very ingenious method. A glass tubes which had been exhausted of air and sealed by fusing its pointed ends, was attached to a sounding balloon in such a manner as to avoid the possibility of absorb- ing hydrogen leaking from the gas -bag. When the balloon attained a certain altitude the closing of an electric circuit by the barometer or by the clockwork of the meteoro- graph caused a little hammer to fall and break one end of the tube. Air entered and filled the tube, which was then sealed by the automatic action of an accumulator, the cur- rent of which heated to redness a platinum wire coiled round the broken end of the tube and fused the glass by the heat thus produced.

div.head: MAMMOTH AND MAN IN SIBERIA.
div.p: MAMMOTH AND MAN IN SIBERIA.

That primitive man was contemporary with the great hairy elephant known as the mam- moth is inferred from certain rude pictures of the animal drawn on bone. Mr. W. Jockel- son-, leader of a Russian expedition in North- East Siberia, concludes that the natives there may have known the mammoth in what must have been more recent times. The Yukaghir of those regions often mention it under the name of Xolhut. It *inferred that the name and their familiarity with the animal are the result of traditions handed down from ancestors who had

div.head: ACTUALLY SEEN THE ANIMAL.
div.p: ACTUALLY SEEN THE ANIMAL.

The natives of this haunt of the mammoth are prepared with a reason for its extinction. It was made too big, they say, and soon ate up all the trees. The spirit of the mammoth, is still, according to their belief, the guar- dian of wizards. It has also a geological sig- nificancy. The world, they say, was originally a flat plain, but the weight of the mammoth wandering over it made the valleys. As an indication of the remarkable abundance of the animal in this part of the world, it may be noted that the annual export of mammoth ivory still amounts to 64,8001 b. This repre- sents the tusks of some 152 individuals. And during the many years the trade has been carried on it is estimated that the tusks of 25,000 individuals have been exported.

div.head: ZODIACAL LIGHT.
div.p: THE ZODIACAL LIGHT.

In the Zodiacal Light we have a vast astro- nomical object requiring no observatory and no telescope for its observation—,and which, indeed, permits none regarding which we are almost, as ignorant to-day as were the astronomers of ancient • Egypt., Doubtless- this is in sonic measure due to the popular fallacy that the light is very elusive and difficult of observation. As a matter of fact, says a writer in the Scotman, it can be seen by any- one possessed of average eyesight who will take the trouble to-look for it on suitable oc- casions. There is no object in the heavens which lends itself so pre-eminently to amateur observation, and it is only by accumulated observations, carefully and systematically made, that its mystery can be finally elucidated. .Of all the forms Which light can take, the Zodiacal Light is one of the most beautiful. It is a

div.head: SOFT AND DELICATE RADIANCE,
div.p: SOFT AND DELICATE RADIANCE,

of gossamer texture, more translucent than nebulce, and not unlike the Aurora Borealis, with which it has often been amociated. It is a conical or lenticular beam which rises from -the eastern horizon in the mornings before the dawn, and from the western in the even- ings after sunset. Although visible -every clear morning and evening within the tropics, it appears to greatest advantage when the ecliptic makes its steepest angle with the horizon, and is therefore best seen in this country at the equinoxes—in the evenings of March and in the mornings towards the end of September.

div.head: WHERE THE LIGHT IS TO BE FOUND.
div.p: WHERE THE LIGHT IS TO BE FOUND.

The broad base of the cone is, always situ- ated just above the sun, and is invariably the brightest part of the light. Its axis, at the times mentioned, makes an angle of about Gfideg. with the horizon, leaning towards 'the south, and lying along the Zodiac—whence the name. Along this medial line the light is much brighter than it is at the edges, and at the latter it fades away so imperceptibly that its exact boundaries are hard to define. Some observers state that this shading off towards the borders is not uniform, but has two dis- tinct gradations—a cone within a cone, so to speak; as if the substance from which the light emanates were condensed along the cen- tral portion, and thinned out beyond. The bulk of the Zodiacal Light is probably somewhat fainter than the Milky Way, but along its brightest parts its brilliance several. times exceeds that of the Galaxy as seen in these latitudes. By contrast, too, with the steel-blue glitter of the latter, the light has a yellow tinge; while at its base a reddish hue is frequently discernible, It has "eemed to some observers that a

div.head: KIND OF PULSATION
div.p: KIND OF PULSATION

was sometimes visible in the light, but this is more probably due either to atmospheric effects or to simple ocular strain. In this country the apex of the light usually extends to a distance of 50deg or 60de„0. from the sun, but on fzivourable opportunities it can be traced as far as 100 deg. On rare occasions, from situations within the Tropics, the Zodi- acal Light has been seen to extend completely round the sky; while on others the light has been witnessed simultaneously at both the east and west horizons, but without complet- ing the round of the heavens.

div.head: PROBABLE CAU3E OF THE PHENOMENON.
div.p: PROBABLE CAU3E OF THE PHENOMENON.

No completely satisfactory explanation of the Zodiacal Light has ye.t been given, and the discussion of its real cause °becomes very difficult, by reason of the want of agreement in the existing 'observations and the conflict- ing evidence at present on record. Certain conclusions may, however, be considered safe. The light is not due to a solar atmosphere, for no atmosphere, in .the proper acceptation of the word, could extend so far from the, sun. Nor is it merely an extension of the corona, for the latter is full of definite struc- ture; while the former is quite devoid of any. Moreover, in coronal photographs there is no trace of any extension 'along, the ecliptic— the long corona' streamers generally lie in other directions. Then, again, the theory that the light is merely sunlight reflected from a swarm of small particles surrounding the earth is

div.head: DECISIVELY NEGATIVED
div.p: DECISIVELY NEGATIVED
by two considerations

In the first, place, there is no parallactic displacement of the cone as seen from dif- ferent places on the earth's surface. And, in the second place, the extension of the cone. to over 100 deg. from tho Sun, and even right round the heavens, indicates that it reaches far beyond the earth's orbit. We are, ,there- fore, compelled to resort to the hypothesis that the light is this to, the presence of myriads of meteorites revolving in orbits round the sun, and extending outside the earth's orbit. The evidence of the spectreseope and the polari- scope so far as it. goes support this theory, as it indicates that the light is mainly, if not entirely, reflected sunlight; and it has . been found that the variations to which the light appears to be subject may be fairly well ex- plained by a crinsideration of the orbite which such meteorites may pursue.

div.head: Latchford Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Latchford Wesleyan Church.

On Thursday evening the annual congregational tea meeting was held in the schoolroom. After tea a mis- cellaneous concert was held presided over by Rev. T. Gladding. The Latchford choir rendered a selection and Mr. Fletcher and Miss Mabel Henshall, songs. Mr. F. Blease and Miss Hartley were responsible for a duet, whilst Mr. Spruce supplied the humorous songs,and Mr. Ford gave a reading. The evening's entertainment was wound up by a sketch entitled "A henpecked husband," the artistes being Messrs. Fletcher apd S, Houghton and the Misses H. Gaskell, N. Ford and E.Ford. On Friday the Sunday school scholars had their innings and prizes were awarded to successful aspirants. Mr. Mails, secretary, presented a favourable report on the year's working.

Bishop of Chester at Warrington. The Bishop of Chester (Right Rev. Dr. Jayne) preached at St. James' Church, Latchford, on Wednes- day evening. Special interest attached to the visit, as Wednesday, being St. Mathias' Day, as well as Ash Wednesday, was the twentieth anniversary of Dr. Jayne's consecration. There was a large congregation. The Bishop based his di. zourse on the words "1 will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven and before thee, and am no more worthy to be called thy son" (St. Luke x.v. 18 and 18). He said that the more they came to realize the character of God as reflected perfectly in life, the sympathy, the ,ufferings, tl'e atonement, and in the victory of Jesus Christ, the more they came face to face with God in Christ, the more they would be drawn to true ter antance. Referrin; to the penitential exercises of almsgiving prayer and fasting, as laid down in the Sermon on almsgiving, Mount, the Bishop said the ruling prir triple wrl that they we.:e not to be ( one for show or from a wrong motive, but to please God. There was no encouragement to ostentation in the Bible. The three duties he had named were bound up together, and not only were they to be done in secret, es unto the Father, but they were all three to be done. In leading the life of dutiful and loving children of God, they must also have that patriotic spirit, that longing to make the world better, to do something to show their penitence was sincere by building up the Church of God.

div.head: Colborne-street Baptist Church.
div.p: Colborne-street Baptist Church.

The Rev. R. E. Letheren addressed himself specially to the young men and women on Sunday evening lest in the Golborne-street Church. lie took as his subject "Plants and corner-stones," and said there was no growth to speak of in plants that were not well rooted. There could be no worthy life that was not rooted in deep convictions. It was what they believed concerning God, and their ielation to Him ; conceining righteous- ness, purity and truth, and their relation to their fellow men that strengthened their life. Tbe height of the stem of loftiness of their ideal would correspond to the depth of their convictions. They should refuse to be stunted by other men's opinions and practices. They should seek to know the truth about life and destiny, and live true to the best they knew. By thought, speech and act they should communicate to their fellows that truth and confidence which were the strength of their own lives. They would never be able to congratu- late themselves on success as appealed to wordly minds; but nothing was so certain as a man whose life was, rooted in great principles, and who reached up to worthy aims, and who had human sympathies, that his life would exert a potent influence on those 'about him. Plants grew up in their youth, and it was in early youth that their character was formed. Ho earnestly beseeched them to think what life they were going to live. They should believe in God and think grandly and greatly of his purpose and plan for their lives. They should believe in Christ for they would find His life the ideal for theirs. All the forces of the universe were working for righteous- ness on the side of men. The s, ...ker then turned to the latter part of his subject and said that corner-stones might 1.3 termed cornices, which was perhaps the cor- r tit meaning. The prominent idea in a coituice was its beauty, so the model of a young woman's life should be a life of beauty. Beauty cif face and figure was a gilt of God, but it was feeble compar with the beauty of character. Tneir life should be ruled by principles end not allowed to be ruined by passions. They should take a share of life's responsibilities. They liked to enjoy themselves and nobody grudged them a wholesome amount of pleasure, but they must remember that life was not a "poppy plot." God only knew the power of the influence that was within the reach of a true woman- hood. Men would always be what women made them and the strengthenibg of society was largely in their hand.

div.head: St. Peter's Church. Annual Tea and Entertainment.
div.p: St. Peter's Church. Annual Tea and Entertainment.

A large number of parishioners gathered on Monday evening last in the scho,)lroorn, St. John-street, on the occasion of the annual tea party and entertainment in connection with St Peter's Church. After the excellent tea the entertainment was begun; and included the following artistes :--Miss Lawless, Miss Lily Glover, Miss Ratcliffe, the Rev. J. H. Garnett, Messrs. Bamforth, G. Greaves, Walker, Taylor, W. Clayton, R. Bennett, Padmore, the choir, and Masters J. Greaves, Sudlow, and Mr. Harry Roberts, humorist. The entertainment was presided over by Mr. Baniforth (vicar's warden), and amongst others present were :--The Rev. B. Percival (vicar), the Rev. J. H. Garnett (curate), Captain Lund (Church Army) and Councillor Steel (people's warden)

The CHAIRALvZsaiiI heat the "cleaning down" of the church would cost £4O. They had not got the money. but they would soon have it, if during the next few weeks the congregation would double the offertory usually given. They had one of the best Vicar's in the town—(applause)—who had always been most straight. forward in all matters connected with the church schools ; while in Mr. Garnett they had a good curate who did his best for all. (Applause.) There was Mrs. Percival—(applause)—she was to be seen going about the parish in all kinds- of weather doing some good work.—ln conclusion, the Chairman asked each member of the congregation to bring at least one person, so as to make tbe congregation a much larger one. (Applause.) Councillor STEEL in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Bamforth said the chairman had rendered valuable, service to the Church, and they were all indebted to him. They wanted the people to pay for the cleaning and beautifying of the church. Their services were bright and cheerful and the sermons good, and he felt convinced that if they wanted money all they had to do was to ask for it, and it would bo forthcoming. (Applause.) The VICAR, in seconding the vote of thanks alluded to how the money was to be got for the renovation and raid they must help themselves and then others would come to their assistance. On the question of Sbcialism he was sure they would rather eat a crust of bread they had earned, not buttered, than have the good things of life taken by force or by any other means from other people that did not belong to them. Ile hoped that that feeling would always obtain, and that the parishion- ers would make up their minds to have nothing to do with that extreme view of Socialism.
The resolution was carried unanimously. Calro-strept Chapel.

It was an interesting event in connection with Cairo-street Chapel, when on Monday last the Rev. Joseph Wood, of Birmingham, paid them a visit. A conf9rence was bold in the afternoon and was well attended. An enjoyable tea was partaken of in the adjoining school. Preaching in the evening to a good congregation, Mr. Wood took for his text " Indeed shall all nations be blessed." Theologians tried to justify the ways of God by the reason that He had a right to do as he liked with His own. Evan as the potter had a right to shape the clay us he Jlhel, zo the Lerd, the great Potter, bad a right to send some to redemption and some to everlasting bell ; and having brought all into existence there was an animate claim for His sympathy, help and encouragement. Continuing, he said they alt started on foundations already laid for them, and which they had no hand in forming. One entered on the race bearing with him refinement, grace and secsi- bilit3, but there were always other forces that tried to drag him down, as by an irresistible effort. Others were born without any of these good qualties. How- ever, they all had a claim, which guaranteed that they would not be cast tiff as rubbish. Election, privilege and favour were only given to the few. Privilege was not given to a man for himself, but for the good of other people. Did they not find that law of privilege at wofit.to-day ? They were as pigmies compared with IVlift _a and Shakespeare in the intellect of the world. 'ere giants so that we might all be blessed. AV cfit had accrued to Society in various we :8 in the a 'ape of lice wledge, discoveriesond inventions" Privilege dlways carried with it duties. The greater the privilege the greater the obligations The more conspicuous the gifts, the Oho imperative the claim of the world upon their service. He was speaking that night to a congregation of elect, privi- leged persons—to a certain privilege in religion. Their thought of God was larger and diviner than others. By them the nations could be blessed. The world was immensely grander than when their fathers lived in it. The new idea of religion was something to share rather than 4o keep. The liberal faith still had gifts for everybody, and it always gave an unspeakable joy to the individual man. They had to face a world of reprcach, of auspicion and rnimepresentation, but the real danger was not there. Their religion w‘ts broad and it was more exacting than tho narrow. The liberal faith was not a power unless it deepened the sense of personal duty, and it would fail unless it was chivalrous. Men had died for calvinism, why should they not die for liberalism, which was a far, grander faith ? There religion was one which called for service. It was for them to make it a positive active force and lead Men- kind. It was not simply for the ministers to help in the deliverence of mankind,but for the people connected with the Cuurch. Service involved sacrifice of time, pleasure, convenience and wealth. They needed to combine individualism with unity and march as an organised force coward.

div.head: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church.

The annual tea meeting was held in connection with the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Thursday. About 170 sat down to a most enjoyable repast, and then adjourned to the chapel to witness the prize distri- bution. The, Rev. E. B. Keeling presided and was supported by lrs. Keeling, Messrs. J. W. Hayward, W. H. Maddock, R. Corbett, Tanner and Farrell. Selections were given by the Silver-street Juvenile Prize Choir undor thd leadership of Mr. W. Hipkiss. Mr. J. E. Hannan and Miss Hilda Hipkiss rendered solos with credit,and Master Tabernacle gave a selection on the violin to the general satisfaction of the audience.

The CHAIRMAN said that from all be could gather the school was one of which they might be proud. As they knew, Sunday schools bad to undergo a great deal of criticism. They were told that the work was waste of time. In Sunday school teaching the work they put into it, the more pains they gave to it, and the more prayer the better would be the result. Whatever was to be done in connection with work of this kind,getting young people to Jesus Christ, there would have to be a good deal, of trouble. There were three rules he was rather fond of and which be could recommend to teachers, parents, Christian workers, preachers, Sunday school secretaries and all the rest of them. The first rule was "Thou shalt not take it easy." If the work cost nothing they might he sure it would not be worth much. The second rule was "Thou shalt not be dull." The third rule was "Thou shalt not despair." This was very.good rule for the Bowsey-road people, when they -had a chairman like him. (Laughter and hear, hear). The SECRETARY (Mr. W. H. Maddock) then read the Sunday school report, in the course of which he said they had had a very successsul year financially and otherwise. He was pleased to say they had retained the (lacers of the school. They had a strong band of teachers. As regarded the scholars, he regretted to have to point out weakness in this direction. They had a larger number of scholars on the books. Taere were 542 scholars-224 boys and 318 girls. The average attendance was only 130 in the morning and 200 in the afternoon. He regretted the continual illness of Mr. Winstanley, and hoped thah he would be able to retain rie post of treasurer which he had held so long. The balance in hand at the end of 1008 was £l4 6s. 6d, Mr. J.W. HAYWARD then presented dressing cases to Miss Healey and Miss Skelland from the Sunday school scholars. Mr. R. CoRBErr also spoke. Mrs. KEELING presented the prizes to tbe scholars. Votes of thanks were heartily accorded to Mrs. Keeling, the Chairman, the speakers and the workers in connection with the tea.

div.head: Warrington Wesleyan Bible Class 'League. Second Annual Gathering.
div.p: The Warrington Wesleyan Bible Class 'League. Second Annual Gathering.

About 100 members and friends of the Warrington Bible Class League sat down to an enjoyable tea, in the Lecture Hall, adjoining the Bowsey-road Wesleyan Church on Saturday evening last, the occasion being that of the League's second annual tea meeting end concert. The after meeting was presided over by Mr. J. C. Holland (President of the League), who wee supported by the Rev. E. B. Keeling, Messrs. C. E. Parker, A. Monnfield and J. Upson. Mr. E. G. RICKERS, the secretary, in presenting his report said it was now about three years since the inception of the League, and the work that had been accomplished since its inauguration had fully justified its existence. There were 11 ' Bible classes affiliated with the League, two of these being composed of the fair sex. During the past year meetings bad been hold at various places and such gatherings could not help but knit closer together the warm feeling of true Christian bre therlin ess, that al ready existed. They had every reason to be proud of the Bible Class League. It had come to stay and they felt sure that its influence would be far reaching. Its objects were worthy of the support of all their Bible Class members, and they were thankful so many were readering what help and assistance they could. Looking back upon the Kist, they could see much that had- been accom- plished,but they did not intend to rest upon past efforts Their motto was "Go forward." _ _ _ _
The TREASURER (Mr. J. Maile). in submitting his report said their income for the last sear was £3O IGs. and the expenditure £32 Is. 6d., leaving a balance of £1 ss. 31d. due to the treasurer.
The reports were unanimously adopted. _

Mr. ,T. C. HOLLAND said it was his desire that the presidency should have gone round. Fos the position to be held two years in succession by the same man had an appearance of monopolisation which he did, not admire. Their organisation was one of the grandest connected with the circuit. The Bible Class League was a brotherhood. Their aim was to promote the influence of social justice and moral purity locally and nationally. (Applause.) FAMr. C. E. PARKER congratulated the League on the election of Mr. Holland to the post of the presidency for tho second time. Mr. Holland had the interests of the League right at his heart and probably the name of the League was written upon it. (I_ iughter.) That was an occasion when they met together to compare notes and to give,counsel between the different classes and suggest new ideas. They at Penketh were going on in a healthy way arel they all appreciated the good that that class did for the iudivideals of it. Perhaps he might mention that they bad commenced in connection with their class a meeting of all the members who cared to attend on one of the week nights,and they had called that gathering together a class fur the study of sociology. They rather felt in their Sunday afternoon meetings that the social question in its various forms was treApassiug- on _ time which the desired to devote particularly to llib;e study and to .other questions of a spiritual and educa- tional character apart from the questions which came under the name of the social question. They had begun this week night class in connection with their Sunday school class for the special study of the many varied phrases of the social and the economic questions so closely affecting their national well being. Ho sug- gested that the idea might be applied to the town branches of the League in some form or other, and also drew attention to the Civic League of Help. He did not wish to press upon them, but he thought it was worth considering whether it was not worth while for their classes as a body to enter in this form of work. He referred to the article in the " Examiner " by Mr. Edmund Osborne on the Guild's of Help Conference in Bolton. Continuing he said he honed everybody would support the "Examiner," which was capable of doing much good work for the progressive cause. Mr. ARTHUR MOUNFIELD spoke very helpfully upon the deep meanings that lay under the parables of Jesue: It was decided unanimously to send a resolution) to the" Daily News," deprecating the appearance of liquor advertisements of late.. Representatives from all the Bible classes spoke of the goodlwork being done by them. Mr. J. UPSON said that the license which had been granted for a public-house7to he erected in Gorsey-lame would be detrimental to their proposals in regard to a new Wesleyan Church close by. He suggested that an executive of that meeting should meet in due time before the Brewster Sessions and should get a list of applications that were to be made for transfers of licences and for new licences and raise on opposition by producing evidence of people nho lived in the district, o organizing petitions against them. The following officers were elected unanimously : President. Mr. J. C. Holland ; secretary, Mr. Fe G. Reliers ; treasurer, Mr, J. Maile ; and auditor, Mr. W. Twiss. - -
Alms HoreroN and Mr, DEAN rendered solos in a highly creditable Manner. A vote of thanks to the Chairman,soloists and speakers °minded the meeting.

div.head: WIFE DESERTION._
div.p: WIFE DESERTION._

At the Boroutih-YOlict-loti-O-n Tuesday, Henrich Sarenson, formerly of Fairfield, was summoned by his wife, Ada Sarenson, St. Mary-street, for desertion and also for neglecting to maintain her. The defendant did not appear. The complainant was represented by Mr. W. 11. J. ;Jenkins. golicitor, who stated that the couple were married at West Derby on the 7th July, 1903. They had two children, Vera 3 years and Catherine 11 months. On the 27th of December the defendant walked out of the !muse and left her. He went qcress to Kilkenny in Ireland, and while there he wrote to the complainant to join him. SI% did so, and on reaching there she found that people were summoning him for debts. He was in the habit of horse betting. Ile had plenty of money but was too lazy to work. He had also pawned all her jewellery. He again deserted her, leaving a note on the table saying that he was sick of the house. He also left the pawn tickets in connection with the jexvellery., The. complaininant had • to sell the furniture in the house in order to redeem the jewellery. She afterwards came across to England again, and her mother and defendant's mother made arrangements to provide the complainant with 103. per week. This was done, but concluded on January last. The complainant then instructed her solicitor to inform her husband that immediate proceedings would be taken if he did not make arrangements for her and her family's main- tenance. When defendant first left her he took all the money. not leaving her a penny to be going on with. Defendant was a good tradesman, and could earn £3 per week easily.—Kate Miller' sister of the complainant, who had been living with her since the defendant left her, corroborated the foregoing statement.—Mr. Jenkins applied for alimony of £1 per week for the complainant. —After some deliberation the application was granted, . the defendant also to pay the costs of the case.

div.head: RAPER BOTTLES.
div.p: RAPER BOTTLES.

Paper bottles for beer, milk, and other beverages, have a _ distinct hygienic value, in view of the fact that they may be thrown 'away after use. They are 'so strong that a weight of 2001 b. will not. crush them. The paper is treated with paraffin, which makes it imper- meable, and also obviates any taste of paper in the fluid. Paper bottles weigh only half as much as glass bottles. A manufacturing plant is said to have been established, and to turn out 200,000 -bottles a day at a price of about a halfpenny apieoe. Sterilised milk, put into these bottles, will remain sweet and free frai bacteria for several days.

div.head: WARRINGTON BUILDING EOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON BUILDING EOCIETY.
Annual Meeting.

The annual :meeting of the Warrington Perznaren Benefit Building Society was held in the Cairo-street schoolroom on Thursday evening. Mr. W. J. Shaw (president) presided and was supported on the platform by :—Messrs. Thomas Ciitchley, John Cooper, S. W. Dallow, C. H. Hibbert, Thomas lace, F. A. Milling, Richard Shackleton, and F. Timporlet (directors), Mr. Aquila Cook (treasurer), Mr. A. J. Willett (solicitor), Messrs. Edwin Bradshaw and W. H. Woodcock (auditors), and Mr.A. H. Clive (secretary).

div.head: TIIE lIEPORT--INCREASED DIVI6ENT.
div.p: TIIE lIEPORT--INCREASED DIVI6ENT.

The Directors, in their forty-second a:na;:al;tatement of accounts, stated that the nett profit on the year's working amounted to £731 195., and the amount brought forward from last year's account was £B2 2s. 5d.: making a total profit of £Bll Is. sd. for distribution., out of which the directors proposed to pay a dividend of R-11 per cent. (free of income tax), to carry £5O to property depreciation account, and the balance for- ward to next year's account. Several sales of property had been effected during the year, and the profit on realisation of same, amounting to £195 ss. 2d., had' been carried to property suspense account, the total credit balance of this account now standing at £659 15s. 7d. The directors again took the opportunity of pointing out the securing of the Society as an invest- ment for further deposits, and hoped the present share- holders would do their best to take up further shares and to introduce new mambers. The directors and officials of the Society were doing so, and they would like to point out th a increase of business in this direction would tend to increase the earning power of the Society, and tho financial position was now so satisfactory that these investments might be made with perfect confidence. The Society was also prepared to make advances on security of desirable properties ill the district.

IThe PRESIDENT, in explaining the report, stated that starting with a balance of £B2 from the previous year, ; they had created a profit sufficient to offer the members the magnificent dividend of 4i per cent, That would absorb about £675 and the money was not as it used to be but it was actually in the bank be drawn upon. When the present Board took over the management of affairs it had been a case of the bank lending to the late Board a matter of nearly £BOO to pay the shareholders a dividend of 21 per cent., and therefore although there had been a reduction in the value of the shades to the amount of 40 per cent.. the GO per cent, that remained in the society was on a firm and sound basis. After paving the dividend they would have a fair and reason- balance to carry forward to next year's account. Although they had been able to pay an additional per cent this year he did not wish the members to go away with the impression that it would be a permanency. Mr. W. H. WOODCOCK, in moving the adoption of the report, said he wished to say a few words which seemed necessary at that particular stage of the society's history- In 1903 they had an awful revelation when they found that £4O out of every £lOO they had invested in the society was absolutely gone and he did not think that I any single member had more to do with the reconstruc- ! tier) of the society than be himself had. He took part in investigations and proceedings and along with hie ! friend Mr. Bradshaw had been an auditor ever since. • They bad striven during the whole of that tires to help- ' the directors in their effort to put the society on a firm, !substantial footing and it was very pleasing that night ' to have Mr. Shaw's assurance that that object had been achieved and that the dividend which had been declared • had been honestly and clearly earned. UnfortunatelYr however, Afr. Shaw went on to indicate that they were not to be too hopeful for the next year. He (Mr. Woodcock) wanted to know why. It seemed to him that after having paid 411, per cent. once they should continue Ito pay it. The work of the society was very much less than it used to be. Since 1903 more than half the property i had been sold, 124 shareholders had been paid off, Etna they now held only £12,000 worth of property, and had ' a share capital of £15,000. In 1902 they advertised for la secretary, and secured the valuable ,services of Mr. Clive at a salary ot £lOO a year, for which be had to • 1 carry out the work of the Society and collect the rents. Subsequently his salary was increased by £2 and they also supplied the office with a telephone, making a total ! payment for salary, office and telephone Lilt per annum He (Mr. Woodcock) submitted that in order to secure the extra per cent, which, having once tasted, they would not be inclined to forego, the expenses ought -to be cut dem:). They bad only houses in Warrington, and they had a special collector for Widnes. It seemed to him that having an income of only £l,BOO from property, and a total number of borrowers of 23, an expenditure of £125 for salary, £l.O for office rent. and £6 ss. for telephone was out of all reason. He suggested to the directors that during the coming year they should 'give careful attention to the subject, so that by strict economy the extra percentage ' might be secured to the shareholders. The Society was to be congratulated on the firm foundation npon which the management of the directors had placed it. and he hoped that by working on the lines he had indicated it would continue to prosper. Mr. JAMES COOK seconded, and said the society seemed to be entering upon brighter days. The report was adopted. ELECTIONS. The ret • (Me

,iring directors (Messrs. S. W. Hallow), W. I. Shaw and F. Timperley) were re-elected, as were also the following oflcials :—Mr. Aquila Cook, treasurer ; win William Twiss, surveyor; Messrs. E. Bradshaw and IW. H. Woodcock, auditors. A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the- . meeting.

div.head: PENKETH.

j LABourt MEETING.—The annual meeting of the local Labour Party was held on Monday evening at the resi- dence of Mr. G. Faulkner.—The Secretary (Mr, J. 3.• Foden) real a report of the year's working, when the various political questions were well debated, aud a plan of the coming year's work was discussed.—The election of a committee and officer was proceeded with, the fo/iowing being elected :—Mr. G. Faulkner, president ; Mr. E. Marshall, secretary ; Mr. J. J. Foden, assistant secretary • committee Messrs. A. Clay, IV. Lesley, W. I Moores, Swift.—The party hopes to hold a series of meetings through the year, and to get the forces well organized by the time the .election comes round, so that the return of Mr. J. Seddon, M.P., may be assured. GITILD MEETING.—In connection with the Wesley Guild, a concert was given by the members of the Pope family, of Gersten. The items were very select and well received by the audience who demanded several encores. Mr. J. Dodds occupied the chair for the first few items, when he was called away and Mr. Johnson officiated in his absence. At the close a vote of thanks was proposed by Mr. Johnson and seconded by Mr. T. Gandy and was heartily curried.

div.head: DEATH FROM ANTHRAX.
div.p: DEATH FROM ANTHRAX.

Coroner Brighouse conducted an inquest at the Borough Police Buildings„ on Monday, on the body of Lawrence Wade, aged 37 years, who died at the Infirmary at a quarter past eleven on the 16th inst from anthrax alleged to have been contracted by falling into a limo pit at the works of Messrs. Waring and Co., , tanners, Winwick-road. Mr. A. Browne represented the widow, Mr. F. G. Taylor instructed by Messrs. Greenall and Co., appeared for Messrs. Waring and Co., and Mr. A. Pearson represented the Insurance Company. Mr. Ashworth, Factory Inspector waioin attendance. The Coroner stated that the irrqUiry was adjourned from the previous Monday in order to make inquiries regarding the poor fellow's death. Mary Ann Wade, widow of the deceased, was called, and said she resided at 6, Winterbottom Lan, Royton Her husband had lodged at 8, Brick-street, Warrington. She received a letter from her husband, informing her that he had fallen in the pit on the 11th inst. Two days latershe received word that he was in the Infirmary,and came over and saw deceased. He did not make any allegations about anything and said to her, "If I die, put your claim in." She stated that deceased com- plained about his throat which was very swollen. There was also a wound on his neck.

George Thomas Plumpton said he was a foreman labourer, working at INlessrs. Wirings' and resided at 33 Chorley-street, Warrington. He had been working for the firm for 21 years and the deceased for about 12 months, Deceased was a joiner's labourer, working on the premises, doing odd jobs. On this particular day a gang of men were repairing a large door at the Dudley-street entrance of the tannery. They were removing this door to another part of the works and four men were told off to carry it. Deceased had hold of the door nearest to the pit and while passing, the door caught one of the principals of the building and jerked deceased into the pit. Witness thought that he went up to his neck. The pit was 5 feet 6 inches in depth. Ha was assisted out of the pit and stood on the side squeezing all the water out of his clothes. In answer to the Coroner, witness said that the hides in , the pit were not British, but he did not know where they came from. Continuing be said that deceased went to his lodgings a short while after wards. Deceased • returned to work the next mornitar, and seemed alright again. On the following Wednesday morning about G o'clock he came to work and complained of a pimple on his nEck. A few hours afterwards he went to the Infirmary and on returning told witness that he had to obtain some clean clothes and go back to the Infirmary as he was suffering from anthrax. In reply to the Coroner witness said there were commodious rooms where the workmen's food and clothing were kept so as to be away from the hides. Soap and nail -brushes were also provided for the con- venience of the workmen who generally washed their hands before leaving work. In reply to the District -Factory Insnector witness said that the pits were cleaned out and fresh curing water was put in after each consignment of hides. They were changed every two months. It was not uncommon for men to fail into the pits, but only two fatal cases had occurred.

Reuben Higbam, manager of Messrs. Waring and Co., sairl thut the hides were imported from Singapore. In reply to questions put by the Factory Inspector he said the anthrax germs could only be exterminated by the burning of the hides or by being enveloped in scalding .steam. Anybody could catch anthrax. Oa one occasion a boil erman working away from the hides caught anthrax from which he died. _ _

Dr. Russell, senior house surgeon at the Warrington Infirmary, said that he made a post-mortem exarnina- lion of the body. On inspecting the wound on deceased's neck he found germs of anthrax which could be plainly seen by the aid of a. microscope. The germs had got into the system and poisoned the blood in the region of the heart. At the same time the man's heart was weak, and was easily overcome by the poison, but had the heart been strong it might have been able to resist the effects of the poison. The Factory Inspeetor stated that he had examined the premises of Messrs. Waring and found them in a satisfactory condition with regard to wasliinr, utensils provided for the workmen, in order to ward off this disease.

The Coroner remarked that the jury had to decide whether the deceased died from anthrax contracted by falling into the pit. Rules were posted up in the works directing that all men who received a scratch, cut, or any injury on the head, neck or arms, should instantly report it to the foreman in order that the wound might be bandaged. They also gave diagrams showing the various stages of anthrax. The Coroner concluded by advising that a large poster should be put up in the works with striking head lines, advising men to report an injury immediately.. Perhaps if the deceased had gone to the Infirmary sooner, his life may have been saved. The jury retuned a verdict that death had resulted from anthrax, contracted by falling into the pit.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

CONCERT AT THE COTTAGE HOMES.—The members of the Warrington .Harmonic Glee Party gave a success- ful concert at the Cottage Homes on Friday evening. An excellent programme was provided, including songs, duets, Ste., and was received with enthusiasm. Several well-known artistes took part. including Mr. Fred Moon, Miss C. Sumner, Mr. W. Gregory (vocalists) and Mr. G. Roscoe (solo pianist and elocutionist). Mr. J. Yates introduced a little variation into the programme with his excellent gramaphone selections. Mr. E. Birchall provided the humorous part of the entertain- ment. Mr. Tom W. Davies was the accompanist. A. hearty vote of thanks was on the motion of the Super- intendent (Mr. A. Wright), passed to the Glee Party on behalf of the inmates and others.

r NURSING AssoCIATION CONCERT.—The Padgato i Nursing Association held their annual concert and ; entertainment at the Council Schools at Padgate on ! Thursday, last week. The programme included vocal and instrumental music and cinematograph exhibition' of pictures. The Misses Bridge and Armitage gave a mandoline duet which was fully appreciated. Miss Lena Duckworth sang " Bring my roses" and "Orange Blossom " earning warm applause. Miss Daintith rendered "A May morning" with effect. Mrs. Jennings was enthusiastically received arid gave a humorous musical monologue "A Railway Guard's Experience " causing uproarous laughter. Mr. Morris sang "Molly the Marchieness "and " Nuggets," to the great enjoy- • ment of the audience. Mr. Blackwell was the accompanist. The Cinematograph exhibition was given by Mr. William Parkinson (Warrington) with his usual skill. It was a treat in itself. Some of the views were of a highly humorous character, while those showing the great undertakings of Canada were of considerable imperial interest and formed a most enjoyable feature of the evening's programme. Farming pursuits of the Dominion were well represented by the cultivation of the laud by ' machinery, harvesting, threshing and other vic.ws of farm work on the prairie. Pictures of lumbering in the forests, and the salmon fishing industries were shown. Also views of the extraordinary feats of rail- way construction including tunnelling through the "Canadian Rockies," abridging precipitions gorges, and making rail-roads on the mountain sides. The cinematograph films were of a very high standard, and were kindly supplied by the Canadian Pacific Rail- way, through their local passenger and freight agent, Mr. Leonard Bennett, 8, King-street, Warrington. The Vicar (Rev. G. W. Dickenson) in the course of his remarks dnrirg the interval announced that the annual meeting of the association would be held on the 17th March, in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Padgate. At the close a hearty vote of thanks was given to all who had taken part in the evenings entertainment. The proceeds will be devoted to the funds of the association.

The went Colliery disaster in Durham brought into prominence many of the advantages enjoyed by the pre- sent generation which were denied to our grandfathers. Within a very short time of the explosion, complete arrangements had been made for the reception and treatment of miners who might be rescued alive. A plentiful supply of food in convenient form was quickly at hand. Large bottles of Bovril were ready for the hot water to transform it into a beverage both stimulating and nourishing. Rescuers and rescued alike wore thus able to appreciate some of the great advan- tages which, science and commercial enterprise have brought close to every member of the community.

(Applause.) When he was considering the vast influence for good which the Queen possessed, 'ar: • Gladstone said ; Row is it that Queen Victoria has this great sway and power • for good " over her people ? Is it power ? No ; still less is it force. Where then does it come from ? It comes, said Mr. Gladstone, from influence. Arid alter all it is the influence of women in so many "departments of life, and particularly in that local government xveich touches the homes and lives of the paonle, which has a power that man cannot attain, and which can never be checked by any Government,- good or bad." In Warrington as in all parts of the Kingdom they had had to face during the winter the unhappy consequenees due to that

were months, and they would suffice if the members oj the League would take advantage of the opportunity, and he earnestly asked that great, p3werful phalanx of labour in Wirrington to help in the work of propaganda, not only on behalf of Free Trade butof the many other groat CIUS439 for whichì. they stood. (Applause.) It was patent that in that greit contest they really had to fight the Press with the platform, aal they hid to do more than that ia Warrington as elsewbere—to meet the power or the parse with the power of the people. (Applause.) If they recognized the facts and used their opportunities, he could assure them that, as far as he was concerned, he would do all he could to get well- informed, able speakers to come to Warrington and put their case 'before the people. (Applause.) He would do his little share of the work as well as he could, for he knew, that in I,Varrington they wore experiencing what was goiug on allithrough the country— a tremendous effort to swamp the whole nation with leaflets and all kinds of misleading, one-sided statements made,perhape, in perfect good faith by some people,others :nada also at the instigation'of people war) were hankering after alO per cent. tariff in order to. , raise the price of the stuff they manufactured and,in the long run, to &sift a coasiderable burden of taxation , from the well-to-do to the poorer classes. (Applause.) A great deal of the movement was very disinterested, he knew but much-if it was interested, too. 0 xing to the immense wealth at the back of the agitation there was no limit to the circular of everg kind of advertising media to the perambulation of. vans through- out the land, and all the arts of that kind. Free Traders must be alive and meet that kind of thing,which was perfectly fair, by enthusiastic work. As the facts were all on their side, they were in a position to beat their opponents hands down]. (Loud applause.) Mrs. Crosfleld then gave two pianafortetsolos in her usual artistic style and was warmly applauded.
