The Warrington Progressive 'Labour League, which rendered such yeoman service at the last general election, is in a very flourishing condition and nutn- bers in its ranks Many enthusiastic advocates of pro- gressive ideals. Proof of the vitality of the organiza- tion was afforded by the large gathering which assembled in the Parr Hall on. Saturday evening on the occasion of the annual tea, concert and meeting in connection with the .League. An excellent tea was served by Atkinson's Cites, Limited, and at the subsequent entertainment a highly interesting musical programme was appreciatively received. The-presence of Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, M.P. and Mrs. Crostield and Mr's. Elijah i lent additional interest to the proceed.. ings and a cordial greeting was accorded them. Amongst others on the platform were : —Mr. J. Elwell, jail. (President of the League), Rev. R. E. Letheren, Mrs. Osborne, Mrs. Simpson, Mrs. Sonner- field, Mrs. Howes, Miss Waywell,Miss Waring, Messrs. C. E. Parker, J. Howes, E. England, S. Wright (treasurer- of the League), J. Morton and J. Howes, jun. (joint secretaries). The artistes were: Emily Taylor and Mr. E. Pownall (sol .ists), the Apollo Prize Quartette, and Mr. B. Hollingsworth (humorist). Mr. T. R. Ford was the • accompanist. All the items were very pleasingly given and the concert was a complete success. During an interval there was some speech-making.
MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH. THE QUESTION OF FEMALE SUFFRAGE.

Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., who was 'enthusiasti- cally received, said that on that platform ho felt he was standing on familiar ground and it would be under any circumstances a great and sincere pleasure to stand face to face with the " jannock " men of Lancashire who fought such a splendid battle on the occasion of that last memorable and truly historic electoral contest they had in Warrington. (Applause.) Tne pleasure was enhanced by the fact that that was the first time he had had, the great -privilege of introducing 'to them the young lady who had linked her fortunes with his. (Applause.) He,thanked them for the kindness of their reception and more especially because he knew it was intended as a hearty Lancashire welcome for his wife. (Apylause.) It was a great pleasure to him also to know that her mother was with them too. (Applause.) It might be risky for him to touch on any of those delicate topics which in his bachelor days he used to hear alluded to occasionally. But still if there were any people present who believed. 'those silly stories .that were sometimes told about the relations between sons-in-law and mothers-in-law, he could only advise them to follow in his footsteps and they would very soon learn their mistake. (Laughter and applause.) It was an unmixed pleasureto come to a fine gathering like that, and to face as he did the representatives of those who, under the leadership of his old friend Mr. Elwell, stood in the very van and fore- front of the Free Trade and progressive forces of the town and were striving steadily and persistently for all that. was best in well ordered yet

COURAGEOUS ,AND THOROUGH-GOING PROGRESS. He was glad to tell them that he felt he could stand there without any notion at the back of his mind that he had got to apologise for half-heartedness or short- comings on the part of a Government which on the contrary, 1.0 believed from the bottom of his heart was thoroughly democratic7-(applause)—fully alive to the sadder side of modern civliFzation and equally determined, so far as it was possible for human Governments to • do • it, to modify those circumstances that were less fair to the people as a whole, and gradually to get rid of economic wrong—a Government which, if ever there was one in this country, was a Government bent upon progress and was deserving of the strong hearty backing of a great progressive League, like that in Warrington. Mr. Crosfield proceeded to refer to Liberal achievements and to some of the great work which lay before the Crevernment. Turning for a moment to ancient history, if one looked back over the last few generations and considered the main character of the work that had been done by the Progressive forces of England, one saw great measures and policies that had been carried through, beginning with the repeal of. the Corn Law in 1846, which opened an entirely now chapter in the domestic life of all the people of this country. Then they passed on to another great era, another land- mark in the history of the progress of England—the adoption Of the Factory Acts—(applause)—and the abolition of

div.head: STUPID, REACTIONARY TAXES
div.p: STUPID, REACTIONARY TAXES

that prevented the natural and free development of the people—such taxes, for instance, as the window tax,and the tax on,newspapers. Other momentous achievements were the institution of the penny postage and the savings bank, and the reduction of taxes upon tea and sugar—and he was sure the ladies, at any rate, would never under-estimate the importance of measures like those, touching the necessaries of life and the comfort of every household. (Hear, bear.) Those were the kind of measures that the as Progressives, as Radicals and Liberals had to look back upon with satisfaction and pride. (Applause.) Turning to the work in which they had been engaged quite recently, there were some matters which would interest their lady friends parti- cularly. Not as a mere proposal but as a practical fact, ' they knew that this year 300,000 of their aged sisters were receiving a pension. (Applause.) That was a reform which deeply concerned the old people, and when they came to oonsider the very young. during that period of their lives when the mothers of England had the entire control of them and in the few succeed- ing years, he was sure all the women present would consider it a reform of the first magnitude whoa we adopted •

- MORE HUMANE AND CIVILIZED METHODS and, once for all, rescued all young offenders in this country from the taint of the Police Court. (Applause.) Various measures were being adopted for the treatment of juvenile offenders and he for one thought it was a noble work, which he was proud to back up. (Applause.) In dealing with the organisation of labour as it affected women, he believed it would be an excellent thing on commercial and still more on humane grounds to regulate the hours of work for weary shop girls. (Applause.) Alluding to women's suffrage, Mr. Crostield said he knew he was on delicate ground and would have to walk warily, but still he would tell them frankly that, as far as he was personally concerned, be had not supported any of the propositions that had yet been • put forward for female suffrage. (Applause.) As he had the privilege that evening of speaking to many of the working women of Lancashire, he would like to say he"was sure that these Duchesses and dainty dames who were coquetting with the ques- tion in London drawing-rooms—he dare say in all sincerity—and who were keen on

FEMALE SUFFRAGE had no 'notion at all of that suffrage being given to their maids and servants and to the working women of Lancashire. (Applause.) It was only right that that should be clearly understood. This tremendous agita- tion for female suffrage and the amount of pressure that was being put on every man-Jack of them in the House of Commons was all very well, but as it was put forward at present it amounted to an extension of the suffrage based on a narrow property qualification, and he must say for his part that was an alteration in the franchise which ho was not going.tosupport-7(apPlause) because al! things considered, he was honestly convinced that they could not have a- Mere reactionary chan !re in this country than a change of that kind. If, on the other hand, the day came when they were faced by a universal national demand for adult suffrage, if women then wished as. a body to take that great additional responsibility upon their 'shoulders, that was a totally different proposition, and he dare say one might have to support that. lle had not said a word yet to try and hurry on a movement of that kind, because what he felt on the subject was 'that at present the whole of municipal work and government was open to the women of this country, and had yet to receive a g reat deal More attention than it'had received from the ladies. He was not blaming women who had so many /responsi- bilities, for deferring this .work, but, if we were going to have, as we might, adult suffrage in the future for the whole population, it was only prudent and natural that in the first instance women might well take ten or twelve years' training in all the different varieties Of local and municipal work, the avenues of which had Item opened to them to a large extent by the present Government. (Applause.) It must. not be supposed that the present Government was against the emancipation Of women, and it he urged that, whatever the solution in the future might he, they might in the first place be content with a littlf+ training in municipal work, he .hoped nobody would suppose he was against

IMtLE E 2,1 ANC IP AVON, • the opening up of everything in professional and even in business earcers and in the whole domain of art to women. "Let the whole field be open " continued ;Ur. Crcsneld, " but .do not let us men, abrogate our own manhood. As business so largely enters into the foreign and home politics of this E ' uipire I tell you quite frankly I think ,it is the duty of men to transact the chief part, to bear the heaviest burden of what is after all a great responsibility—the government of the country—but let women take a large share in that government too. -Don't- let us prejudge the future. After this training in municipal work has been gone through, the Otitrate solution, I know, may be adult suffrage. lam quite sure that it is a mistake to try and rush a Measure of that kind at the present time, but I do feel most strongly that if we do not have that, it is all, the more. incumbent on every man in politics to , view every single question that

div.head: UNFORTUNATE E 133 I TRADE
div.p: UNFORTUNATE E 133 I TRADE

which in England, as in other countries' we occasion- ally had to deal with. We in England had been con- fronted with what had been . felt in a much more terrihle'way in America and also 'to a very serious extent in Germany—that saddest of all problems, unemployment. He was glad to be able to endorse what he said in that hall last autumn, that there was no question on which the minds of the Government were bent more than upon this problem. •It was, in fact, in the minds of the whole Liberal party. There was no make-believe in the sympathy that was felt, he could assure them. He believed the Government was on the right lines in making a painstaking investigation not into one remedy alone bet into many different schemes by which they hoped finally to reduce almost if not entirely to vanishing point the terrible evil of unemployment and the still sadder problem of the unemployable. It might be asked how an

IRISH LAND DILL could act as a remedy? They heard Mr-. Birrell from that very platform described how he hoped to tackle that difficult question of the congested districts of the West of Ireland. Well, it was largely from those districts that we got 40,000 or 50,000 Irishmen coming across the water every summer to dud work in England and to a great extent in Lanca- shire and Yorkshire. Only that week %tr. John Burns had ,"eclared in the House of Commons that if that measure were successfully dealt with and land purchase in Ireland carried throng, so that the Irish peasant stayed in his own country, seven-eighths of the difficulty of casual labour at the Liverpool docks would be got rid of. (Applause.) There had also been a most interesting discussion on a question of which they had heard a great deal for months past—that of finding additional employment by means of afforesta- tion, and Sir Charles Dilke, with his encyclopedic knowledge, criticised very usefully the report of the Commission which had sat upon that question. He (Mr. Crosfield) was sure that anybody who attentively followed Sir Charles' criticism would realize that the question had to be faced with discrimination. However, he was happy to say. that the upshot of the debate left in his (Mr. Crosfield's) mind the conviction that there was a groat deal of useful work that could be done by the State in the way of

AFFORESTATION —work which he most certainly would support.(Applanse. The chief reason was that the returns from afforestation were often so long deferred—perhaps for forty or fifty years—that they could not expect s private employer to invest his capital in work of that kind and as a general rule the private employer did not do co. The State, however, could afford to be out of its money for that length of tine and in many cases work of that kind could tre carried out on the Royal property, then there was

div.head: HOUSING 'IN THE RURA.L DISTRICTS.
div.p: HOUSING 'IN THE RURA.L DISTRICTS.

They must feel that proper lik.;;;;Iii-g-i-n-ii-Ser places WAS the first step to making a man with a little ambition and enterprise satisfied to cut out his own career in his own country district instead of swelling the stroam that drained the country and helped to make the demand for work all the more serious in the industrial centres. Rural housing, if properly tackled, was from the point of view of unemployment an extremely important thing. Of course, in dealing with the physique and health of the nation, we as town dwellers had first to think about our slums. (I-fear, hear.) We must get rid of the slums all through England and he was certain all progressives would feet strougly that, to use a familiar phrase, they. could wit raise an imperial race out of rookeries. The question touched the .very life-blood and well-being of the whole nation. As to rural hous- ing, he was firmly convinced that that was one of the indirect but none the less sure measures for. solving unemployment. (Applause.) He had heard deprecatory remarks made in the House about -

LABOUR BUREAUX to give information to employers and employed, so that any deficiency in labour in one part of the country could be remedied from another quarter where there was redundancy. But in spite of what was said, he thought Germany had done very well in that respect, and the recent report of Mr. Henderson and Mr. Barnes showed the value of labour exchanges which, if adopted, would he beneficial to the workers of this country. He could not think of anything more dis- tressing than a workingman making a long journey on a false scent and that was the main thing which labour exchanges would prevent. Then there was the question of wages boards, not to interfere with the great industrial organizations we had in England where labour was able to keep its end up and make its own bargain ; he would not favour any such interference,for he was not one of those who thought that the State could do everything. (Hear, hear.) He had seen thu Ministers at work in the House of Commons; and he knew how bard put to it they were to get through their duties and he would be very sorry indeed for a President of the Board of Trade or the holder of any similar position who ever tried to tackle that work when the State attempted to run the whole show itself. (Laughter.) "If you ask me thy opinion" added Mr. Crosfield "I think the unlucky mortal who ever does that will just break his back." (Laughter.) It would be the greatest possible pity to interfere where the balance of power had been so nicely adjusted, where the various interests wore fairly considered through thcse big organizations, but he was equally thankful to know that the State was going to interfere in order

TO PROTECT THE WEAK. He could never forget that passage in " The history of civilization" where Buckle, who was a most unqualified individualist and strongly opposed to all Government interventbn, laid down as one of the essential (MUGS of government—" the protection of the weak from Oppression. by the strong." If that was - true in his day, it was true now. (Hear, hen.) He (Mr. Crosfiel(i) was sorry to hear only the other day that even in War- rington there were cases of what he considered nothing less than oppression of that kind. He would rather not give them a name and he would not do so that night, but he stated the fact,—because he knew it was a fact—cf juvenile labour -being exploited in a certain industry in a way that ought to be instantly stopped. (Applause.) H 3 did not suppose there was any oily in. the Kingdom where they would find worse cases of that than in some parts of London and where that kind of thing obtained be was thankful to say they were going to institute -these boards which would regulate the conditions by fixing a minimum wage. The abolition of sweating would have a great effect on unemployment, because the spending power of those poor people who were at present working under unfair conditions would be increased, and consequently-the general consumption of articles of utility would he greater and the demand would be extended. (Applause). Without promising fancy wages,the Government would endeavour to do what was fair in the matter, and if they brought about an improvement on the one hand, were they, on the other, going to

DINtINTSTI TITE SPENDING POWER of the people by raising the price of everything they bought, whether necessarieS or luxuries. under what- ever pretext ? (Cries of "No.") Mr. Crosfielcl emphasised the hollownns of the Protectionist argu- ments as advanced in the debate in the House. No doubt in dealing with intricate economic problems there was the possibility of the public being gulled to a 'considerable extent, unless the theories of the Opposition were met ,with the facts and that was where the Progressive labour League could be of great service. The FreA Trade case was all above board ; they had nothing to conceal.' A great deal cf fencing and skirmishing, and evasion and dodging of the issues. was going on all .round amongst the Tariff Reformers. That was ncit the position of Free Traders. They were willing to face the music—(applause)--and he was truly glad to hear in London that day that they in Warrington were so ready to do so, that his friend Mr. Morton sent

div.head: LITTLE CHALLENGE
div.p: A LITTLE CHALLENGE

the other day. (Applause.) Certain side issues were raked, but when it came to the point be thought the challenge was not going to be accepted. He called that pretty significant, and if the tariff reform party in War- rington would not face the proposed public discussion, well, they as Free Traders were. independent of them. There were many months, perhaps a year, perhaps more between new and the next election. At any rate there
'ac;

div.head: "GLORIOUS _DAYS."
div.p: "GLORIOUS _DAYS."

Mr. J. Howns said they ware Radical Free Traders, and such they intended to remain. Their Tory friends said they only wanted to put a small tax on food. Well, we could not afford a small tax. (Hear, hear.) Tariff Reformers said they did not want to tax raw material. Free Traders replied : " Food is raw niaterial for the production of human beings." (Applause.) The Tariff Reformers were great at imperial issues, but the great- ness of the Empire did not depend upon its extent; but upon the condition of its people. The present Govern- ment had passed a magnificent measure in the Children's Bill.(Applause.)Prom the first of April no British child would go to prison. (Applause.) If the LiberarGovern- meat had done nothing more than that,they deserved the confidence of the people. (Applause.) Homes would be spozially provided where youthful offenders. would be educated and trained, and everything Would bo done to keep them clear of the taint of criminal life and give them a chance in the world. He did not know whether that Bill was not going to do S great deal for the industries of the town, for there would certain!y be a great boom in fireguards. (Laughter and applause.) The Government had done some glorious work in pro- tecting tke children and making provision for the aged. There were some old age pensioners present at that meeting. (Applause.) These were glorious days and they were glad to think that Warrington ha&a hand in doing that work. (Applause.) After travelling for over twenty years in the deserts of Toryism, they emancipated them- selves at the last election and returned a gentleman of whom the constituency might well be proud.(Applause.) Alluding to the Labour League's challenge to debate, Mr. Howes said the League did not confine it to War- rington but invited their opponents to select the hest man they could find in the country. The Tariff Reformers were wise in their generation and conse- quently they did not intend to go on with it. (Applause.) WARRINGTON AND TARIFF REFORM.

! Mr. J. EL WELL in proposing a vote of thanks to the artistes and the ladies Who bad assisted at the tea tables, showed how the Government had already carried out some of the most important items which the League included in its programme on its formation five years Lago, such as the Trades Disputes Bill, old age pensions, and small holdings and allotments. He claimed that the Government, had done more for the poor and the work ineelasses than any Conservative Government to his knowledge. Tariff Reformers, in advocating their scheme as a solution of unemploy- ment, pointed to the vast quantities of steel that came into Warrington. What) would be the result if a 10 per cent tariff were imposed? lie would ask any employer in Warrington who used blooms and billets from abroad,whether he wanted al9 per cent. tariff putting on. (Cries of" No.") He knew for a fact that they did not want it. If they took the average cost of billets and blooms at £4 per ton, a ten per cent, tariff would be about Bs. The consequence would. be that the finished article would be considerably dearer and we should be hindicapoed in the neutral markets of the world. Then again, we sent Germany 31,000 tons of tin plates last year. Steel blooms cost about Zi per ton but tin plates cost something like £l2 or ,C:,14 per ton. We sent them 10,000 totA of black sheets for tinning and considerably over 1,000 tons of galvanised sheets. The tin plate and sheet trade was practically the highest and best paid portion of the iron and steel trade of this country. Mr. Elwell con- tended that the iron trade was a diminishing quantity, owing to the increased demand for steel, and no amount of tariff would bring it back to its former condition.He as a workman would never give his vote for a policy that would raise the cost re the necessaries of lite to the poort st of the land. (Applause.) Mr. J. MORTON seconded and said he was sure they could all endorse Mr. Crosileld's views on women's suffrage. Thenernber had outlined some important developments which the Gtoverntnent had in view, deal- ing with many great social problems. They had before them a fight sirnilaT to the one at the last general election. They had to fight the Protectionist question again and return a representative of Free Trade principles. (Applause) The vote was heartily passed. MR. AND M 11,3 CROSFIELD T [TANKED.

Mr. S. WRIGHT then propased a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. and Mrs. Crosfleld for their presence. Mr. E. ENGLAND, in seconding, said Mr. Crosfield was a member of a family which ad always served War- rington well in its day and generation. Long might that family prosper and might it always have some part in representing the Liberal interest in Warrington. (Applause). The vote was passed with enthusiasm. div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " The Village Blacksmith."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " The Village Blacksmith."

That old favourite "The Village Blacksmith " is presented at the Royal Court Theatre this ueek by Messrs. Dottridg,e, Longden, and Livesey's comPany. Nightly the brawny smith wields his hammer in the picturesque village smithy of poetic fame, and goes through many startling adventures not thought of by Longfellow. In the eyes of the gallery habitu‘s the man of muscle is a veritable hero. They are almost moved to tears by the .destruction of his happy home- life through the vile conspiracy of Captain Leo, and execrations are heaped on the head of the remorseless villain. What cheers rend the air when the captain is vanquished in the wrestling match by his much-wronged opponent! This combat of the giants is looked upon as the tit-bit of the play. Both men are fine specimens of physical culture, as well matched as the most ardent enthusiast could desire, and the audience watches the contest with bated breath. It is quite a relief when the blacksmith triumphs and the curtain is rung down to the accompaniment of joyous acclaims. The company is a thoroughly capable one and infuses great spirit and earnestness into the performance. %%Sam Livesey,is an ideal John Strong, the village blacksmith; indeed the part seems to have been created for him. Of fine presence and manly bearing, the frank, hearty manner traditionally associated with the character is assumed to perfection. Mr. Albert Sinclair does equally well ia the somewhat thanklesss role of Captain Leo, his portrayal being finely realistic. Miss Maggie Edwards is sufficiently pathetic as Kate Strong and Miss Cassie Le Grande's touching interpretation of Ruth Parkins is worthy of praise. Two clever studies are those 'of Mr. Thomas E. Marshall and Mrs. T. 0 Livesey who play the travelling tinker and his wife as to the manner bOrn. The play is relieved with plenty of rollicking fun for which &Er. Fred Miming as Billy Twigg,a country bey,ancl Miss Edith Gicklens, as Martha llopps, are chiefly responsible. Mr. Edwin Maydew is a capital Lucas Mailer and Miss, Kathleen Saunders wins all hearts as little Harry Strong. NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. Mr. C ROSFIELD, in responding, emphasised the fact that-tariffs would raise prices all round, and therefore increase the cost of production, and so to a certain extent check our vast preponderance of trade in so many foreign maakets, and particularly in the great neutral markets of the world. That applied especially Co the greatest of • all Lancashire industries, for the trade which Lancashire cotton manufacturers did in the neutral markets was the amazement of the whole world. A great deal of our cotton trade no doubt was held very securely, but there •came a point where the British manufacturer was met very closely by the American. • Why was it that we held this trade of millions upon millions, to-day.? The answer was quite simple. The foundation of all our gigantic over- see trade, whether in cotton or in the case of smaller industries like the one with which he bad the honour to he connected, was low cost of manufacture. The raising of prices by tariffs would inevitably lead to a reduction of trade ; with reduced output would come further increased cost of manufacture owing to all standinper charges and cost of management pressing more heavily upon manufacturers. gash and reckless promises of more employment and better wages had been made without any foundation. He would ask. them whether under such circumstances manufacturers would be either willing or able to pay higher wages to their workpeople, or whether on the • contrary diminished trade in the great neutral markets would not be much more likely to lead employers to demand a reduction in wages-in order to keep dowa their cost of manufacture and enable thorn to retain their trade in those markets. Hence Protection, by raising the cost of all commodities and diminishing the purchasing power of the people at home and cutting into our over- see trade, would not-only increase instead of diminish- ing unemployment at home, but would tend to cause very serious friction between employers and employed as well. Next week we shall corn. A FOREWORD mence a new issue of the AB)IIT THE "Examiner," which will be pages,
" EXAMINER." enlarged to ten

altered to a more convenient and handy size, and published with the pages cut at the top, BO that the reader will have easy access to the news in all parts of the paper. We have installed special machinery in order that we may be in a position to issue the paper in a smart, attractive, and thoroughly up-to-date style. It will be our aim to make the " Examiner" the people's paper, as well as the leading Liberal and Progressive weekly journal for Smth-West Lanca- shire and North Cheshire. Tne local news of the week will be set out in a bright, intelligent way, and special featutes will be introduced to cater specially for the widely differing tastes of various circles of readers. Those who appreciate good fiction will Welcome our new serial story by such a famous and popular writer as Max Peelber- ton- "The Show Girl" is his latest novel, and the opening chapters appear in our next Saturday's now issue. Then there will be a prize scheme for the _football enthusiasts, and topical illustrations which should appeal to and interest all. A weekly article entitled My Life Story" will be con- tributed by prominent local men, His Worship the Mayor leading the way. A literary section will receive special attention, and among the regular features of this page will be a series of historical and antiquarian articles dealing with aspects of Warrington of the past. These will be written under the general ' title " Warrington Chapters" and will be con I tributed by Mr. Arthur Mounfield, The series will begin with an interesting account of Lewis Carroll and his wonderland. All the world has read "Alice in Wonderland" and it has been translated into meat European languages and even into Arabic, but few people know where the original Wonder- , land lay. Warrington readers will Ise interested I to learn that Wonderland is on a pretty hill top within sight of their own town. Among other articles which have been prepared for this section are ehapters on "Early Roman Catholic Worship in Warrington," " Warrington and the Civil War,' "The story of St. John's Presbyterian Church." These wld appear during the next few weeks. The " Examiner ' will thus join the many-sided War- rinton of the past with the no less versatile Warrington of the present, and we believe that the chapters will be worthy of the famous old town they will describe. Our Literary section will also contain a "Miscellany" to which interested readers may contribute their opinions or memories, and co-operate with our contributors to the enhance- ment of the paper. We feel both hopefel and confident that under its new regime the "Examiner' will surpass all its previous achievements, and secure an even warmer and more valued place in the esteem of the people of Warrington and district.

The Borough Member's MR. CROSFIELD sympathy with Labour AND LABOUR aspirations and progressive POLITICS, ideals generally is well known, and he is never happier than when addressing a working-class audience. Oa Saturday evening Mr. Crosfield gave further proof of the deep interest which he takes in the fortunes of the Progressive Labour League by attending the annual social gathering of that flourishing organization at the Parr Hall and delivering an able speech on some of the great q nestions of the day. The present Government is above everything else, thoroughly demoeratic, and Mr. Crosfield convincingly demonstrated the determination of the Ministry to still further advance the cause of true progress and to remedy social ills. As to their recent achievements, the passing of the Old Age Pensions Act, to which the Member alluded, should be sufficient to entitle them to the gratitude of the nation, and—what is of equal importance—they have shown themselves to be alive to the best interests of the rising generation by placing the Children's Act upon the statute book. It would be difficult to over-estimate the importance of both these beneficent measures,which will bring well-deserved comfort to the aged and help to safeguard the nation's most precious asset—the children. The future is fraught with many problem of serious import, but overshadowing every- thing is the tragic question of the unemployed. Mr. Crosfield discussed a number of indirect remedies—such as aftorestation, the Irish Laud Bill, rural housing, and wages boards—which are certain to figure prominently in efforts to arrive at a solution, and hit remarks under these heads are worthy of thoughtful attention. Well con- sidered measures of this kind would undoubtedly do a great deal to mitigate the evil and bring about a brighter era for those to whom poverty is a perpetual menace. Mr. Crosfield rightly took occasion to condemn the reckless misrepresenta- tions of the Tariff 113forraers. The effect-of their policy would be to shift a considerable burden of taxation from the well-to-do to the poorer classes and by increasing the cost of production it would lead to diminished trade, less employment, lower wages, and to serious friction between employer and employed.
There must be some uneasy consciences in the T ,ry
WHY D ) MR

TORIES SQUIRM P party judging by the indications of the last few days. In our last issue ye turned the light upon some of the wheels within wheels which moved the proceedings for the unseating of Mr. P. Peacock to take the course they did. We pointed out the very important and incontestable fact that in bringing the petition and setting up a Court in Warrington the Tory party had taken the most expensive and cumbrous method of making their lofty moral protest against bribery and corruption in municipal elections. They involved the town, in the most reckless and incon- siderate fashion, in an expense estimated at £l,OOO, over and above the costs which naturally fall upon the parties to the petition. It was open to them to take proceedings in the Assize Courts, and if their case was a good one they had-nothing to lose thereby, while the town would have been the gainer by a saving of about £9OO. We Understand that the proceedings in the Gough case of bribery did not cost the town more than £6O. Apparently our Tory friends would rather we had overlooked the serious issue for the ratepayers of the great petition. But even "The Observer " g ive its friends away by saying: " We are informed that the cost which the electi,on will entail on the ratepayers will be from £BOO to £1,000." Our discreet contemporary, the " Guardian," with a close observance of that neutrality which seems to be entirely opinionless, made no eomment at all about the petition, it results, or its cost. The Tory party, regardless of facts, persists in its folly, and this week the hoirdings have been decorated by the appended effusion in

div.head: RADICALS
div.p: THE RADICALS
are saying that the Tories have cost the town £l,OOO by the Election Petition. THIS IS NOT TRUE. IT Is TETE LIBERAL CANDIDATE, PETER PEACOCK, BY MS AGENTS
who has caused this expense by the corrupt practices of , BRIBERY AND CORRUPTION.
THE ELEOTORS OF WARRINGTON WILL KNOW HOW TO PUT THE SADDLE ON THE RIGHT HORSE,

This is drawing a red herring across the trail with a vengeance, but like 0.)lonel Hall Walker, we can see through it. Its transparency is obvious almost to the blind. The Tory party brought the petition and the petition cost the town £l,OOO. The " Observer " also affirms the fact as we have shown. Mr. Peacock was prepare(' to defend the action either here or at the Assizes. The cost to the town was a matter entirely out of his control. If he had been proved guiltless the town would still have had to pay, and for no other reason than that the Tory party chose to saddle the ratepayers with an inquiry lasting twelve days to prove five skillingsworth of bribery and treating. We hardly think the public can be gulled into believing that Mr. Peacock was so perfidious a person that he bribed his electors and then involved them in an expense of £l,OOO to prove it. As to " putting the saddle on the right horse "—first find the horse. Personally, we should look for it in the 'Tory stable!

1 Cemmercial affairs of QUESTIONABLE considerable national and COMPANIES. local importance were discussed at the anniial meeting of the Chamber of Commerce on Thursday and we regret that the pressure of other local events prevents U 3 giving a full report of the proceedings. 0114 point was raised which we feet impelled to touch upon, as • the subject has been much in the public mind of late. We refer to that class of limited companies known as investment, bond, savings, or mortgage companies. Mr. C. D. Parkinson drew the Charnbar's attention to , these concerns, the operations of sorae of which he said were sometimes of a fraudulent nature and demanded the attention of Chambers of Cimmene quite as much as other branches of trading and industry. He mentioned that he had previously been in communication with the B )ard of •Trade on the subject, and it was being closely investigated. The question is one which, as he rightly pointed out, touches very nearly the *wel. fare of the poorer classes. Revelations of the intolerable hardships imposed- on poor and thoughtless investors in this class of company have recently been made in the Manchester County Court before Judge Parry. We notice that attention was drawn to the matter in the House of Commons on Thursday by Mr. Joynson Hicks, M.P., and Air. Churchill, the Pr*iident of the Board of Trade, gave a reply which showed that his department was fully alive to the necessity for safeguarding the savings of the thrifty poor. ,He was, he said, considering the advisability of , ' introducing a bill placing bond investment corn- panies and house-purchase nompanies under ' conditions somewhat analagous to those which are now imposed on life assurance companies. Such a provision is an imperative necessity, and one which the Chambers of Commerce may well advocate with all the energy of which they are posclessed.

The above heading is one Tgicamts AS which doubtless attracted Weiragssga. the eye of many readers of a certain evening piper this week. The over•crowded state of the teaching prole3sion furnishes a national problem not easy of solution. Young teachers are contiuually passing through the colleges, only to fiod that there is no opening for thorn in the schools.

At the meeting of the Essex Bducation Com- mittee it was decided to defer proposals for pro- viding a county training college for teachers owing to the fact that so many college-trained teachers were unable to and plaees. Figures weie quoted showing that out of 2,600 passing out of college 1,000 had not found places in three months. The Rev. Murray Aynsley, principal of llockerill College, said that many students had been compelled on leaving oollege to become waitresses at City restaurants Ind take on odd jobs at stores and drapery establishments.

There is something almost tragic in a statement like the above. That students should be induced to pass through an expansive training to qualify for the teaching profession and then find them- selves among the unemployed is a sad reflection on the national administration of E lucation. It is high time there was sciale comprehensive scheme evolved for regulating supply and demand. lie leas than 4,000 teachers came out-of the Training Colleges in July next, and there seena.s little hope of any more than a small percentage of them find ing employment in the schools. Sixteen Warring ton girls will be included in the number—and tkere are no vacancies or prospective vacancies in the Warrington Schools! Are these trained and qualified teachers to be driven into the restaurants and drapery stores to earn a meagre living at a class of work wherein their special talents and ability will be totally wasted ? Seeing that the difficulty is this brought to our own doors, the question of the employ nent of married women teachers needs to be considered solely on its merits, or demerits, with sentimental considerations rigidly excluded. There are ten married women teachers in Warrington scho and their situations will be claimed, and rightly in our view, by the sixteen local students who come out of college in. July next. Had Mr. Bradbliaw's resolution been carried at the last meeting of the Education Committee the way would have been clear; meanwhile the Committee is hesitating. We can only remind them that they must be just before being generous,and it is justice only that is demanded by the young teachers who have been induced to qualify for an exacting and responsibleofpis on.

Dr. Chavasse was talking of the great good vihich the Fund did in advancing loans in necessitous cases, but when he proceeded to add that they were lent at a " row late "of interest, even the most sedate of his auditors could scarcely ,refrain from smiling. Princess Trixie, the " thinking " horse, which has been killed in America, had travelled the world, and was for a long time on tour in this country. She made a lengthy stay at the White City, Manchester. A fine white Arab, she was of " show " stock, both her parents having been performers. Princess Trixie's cleverness gave rise to much controversy as to whether she really had the thinking faculty or not, but there was no reason to suppose that her cleverness was due to anything more than a careful training. There was none of that originality or departure from set actions which betokens thought. * * * Flying does not seem to be nearly as dangerous as motoring.—King Alfonso. We have had enough of war, and want all our time to pursue our peaceful vocations.—Mr. Kato the new Japanese Ambassador. What is the great secret of unemployment that is so prevalent both East and West? It is lack of character. —Father Bernard Vaughan. I can conceive no higher role for a University than to complete its work by enlarging the sphere of its teaching so as to put before the minds of its students the study of national defence, without which no nation can feel secure.—Mr. Haldane, Secretary of State for War.

Charles Dickens, were he alive to-day, would welcome the approaching extinction of the workhouse with fe-31ings of heartfelt gratitude. Against that nightmare of poverty he waged an incessant warfare. One recalls that fierce outburst in " Our Mutual Friend " : -" This boastful handiwork of ours, which fails .in its terrors for the professional pauper, the sturdy breaker of windows aod the rampant tearer of clothes, strikes with a cruel and a wicked stab at the stricken sufferer, and is a horror to the deserving and unfortunate. We must mend it,Lords and gentlemen and honourable boards, or in its own evil hour it will mar every one of us." Those words were written in 1803, and it has tAlten forty-six years to accomplish the reform for which Dickens so strenuously fought. * * *

A number of distinguished men in different walks of life were recently asked by Mr. A. B. Cooper to say what in their opinion is the most magwficent passage in the Bible. The replies are published in the March " Sunday at Rome," and are very intesest- ing. Mr. William Watson, the poet, says : Whole chapters of Isaiah, such as xl. and lx., are simply clusters of passages that touch the highest levels _of grandeur, and every kind of literary

magnificenCe is supremely exemplified in the Bible-. The most perfect elegy in all literature, Ifr- Watson adds, is perhaps David's lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam. 1., 19-27), and at the other end of the great gamut of emotion is the song of Deborah and Barak (Judg. v., 2-31), " the most superb expression of the intoxication of triumph that I know." * * _

Correspondence which has been issued as a Parlia- mentary paper regarding the weekly rest-day shows that is only within the last few years that legislation on the subject has been attempted in any of the countries from w'tich reports come. Germany and Denmark led the way in 1904, Austria and Holland followed in 1905, France and Switzerland in 1900, and legislation in other lands is of even more recent date. The French experiment is perhaps the most interest ing of all. Our Embassy reports that its effects " are evident to the most superficial observer uf French life." The closing of the large shops has not caused the people to fall back up:m the establishments, bet is inducing them to do their shopping on week-days. And so in time the small shops will probably come into line, and the French Sunday may not differ so very greatly from the much-abased English Sabbath.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
ASSAULT ON WIDNES POLICEMAN.

Thomas Cain, a young Widnesian, was charged at Widnes, on Monday, with assaulting Police Constable Stevenson while in the execution of his duty on Satur- day last. It was stated that tkeconstable was struggling with another man on the way to the police station, and while in Waterloo-road the prisoner, who had been asked to give assistance, came up to the constable and gave him a punch in the face, and knocked his helmet oil. When charged in the police station with assault, he commenced to threaten Stevenson. Police Constable Tobin, who was in company with Stevenson, corrobor- ated. Inspector Burton also explained Cain's conduct while being put into the cell. He was very much the worse for drink at the time. He had been before the court on seven occasions previously for assault of various descriptions. Prisoner denied all the know- ledge of assault, and said he assisted Stevenson and Tobin to the police station with their charge. The bench said the case was clearly proved against him, and he was fined 20s. and costs.

div.head: LEcrung ON IRELAND.
div.p: LEcrung ON IRELAND.

On Thursday evening last week, the Rev. James Cregan, the well-known Manchester preacher, gave a most interesting lecture at Newton Congregational School, on " Ireland: its beauty, song, and humour." He said some people living not far from Newton had a continual fear that if they went to Ireland they would be killed flve minutes after landing. This was a mis- take; they would be killed every minute they stayed there—with kindness. He would dispel many of the illusions people had in regard to Ireland and the Irish. They were just like other people, but more handsome and intelligent. Yet they were a strange iecom- prehensible race, with aspirations and ideals John Bull would never understand however long he tried to govern Ireland. Thanks were tendered at the close, by the Rev. J. Davidson, who presided over a large company.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, conducted an inquiry, at the Railway Hotel, Earlestown, on Thurs- day, into the circumstances surtouuding the death of George Wilson, 56, a waggon-maker, of 12, •Lawreace- street, Earlestown. From the evidence it appeared that on Saturday morning Wilson, who had not worked for same time, owing to illness, said he was going upstairs to shut the windows. His daughter was, however, suspicious, and she prevailed upon her mother to follow him. On reaching the bedroom Mrs. Wilson saw her husband standing in front of a mirror with a pocket-knife in his hand, and at her approach be drew the knife across his throat from ear to ear.
Medical aid was summoned, but death occurred the next day. Dr. Harrison, who attended deceased, said that the jugular vein had not been severed, and he was of opinion that death was due to the shock.
A verdict of ' Suicide whilst of unsound mind" was returned.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
MEASLES EPIDENIIC AT ST. HELENS.

The St. Helens health report shows an increase in the death-rate during the past fortnight, from 19-3 to 2.1•3. There have been 16 deaths from infectious disease, measles accounting for nine. Seventy new cases of sickness are reported, apart from 172 cases of measles against seventy-eight in the previous two weeks. The birth-rate is 35•2.—Dr. Buchanan, at the meeting of the Health Committee, said he had found it necessary to advise the closing of the infants depart- ments at eight schools, viz., Sacred Heart, Lowe House, St. Thomas's (Denton's Green), St. Thomas's (Lyon street), St. Peter's (Parr), Knowsley-road, St: Teresa's (Newtown), and Nutgrove Wes!eyed. They would all be closed for three weeks. Scarlet fever was diminish- ing, but measles were very prevalent. He found it impossible to visit all the eases with the ordinary staff, and asked the committee to appoint a special nurse to help until the epidemic abated.oa the last occasion they took one of the nurses from the sanatorium, and gave her extra remuneration, and Med up her place at the sanatorium temporarily.—The committee decided to adopt this course.

div.head: REBUILDING A ST. HELENS CHURCH.
div.p: REBUILDING A ST. HELENS CHURCH.

St. Thomas's Church, St. Helens, was on Sunday evening packed with parishioners when the last evening service was held previous to the nave of the church being pulled down in order that a new structure may be erected. The church was built in 1839. and about six- teen years ago, owing to its ruinous condition, a new chancel was built and the nave restored. Since the Rev. Leonard J. Rich became vicar, eleven years ego funds have been accumulated for the new nave. The work has been commenced, and the cost will be about £B,OOO. The church is the only one in the town possessed of a full peal of bells, and these were specially rung before and after service for the last time. The evening service was of a special character, and the vicar preached, and said there was a double task laid upon them of maintaining their organisation and of rebuild- ing their church. It would test their faith, their loyalty, and their courage, and.he trusted that next year, when they opened with joy and gladness their new church, they would be renewed and strengthened, that they would have stood the test, and that their loyalty and numbers would be increased.—At the con- clusion of the service a recital was given by Mr. W. P. Biyliff, organist, and the choir. During the rebuilding of the nave Sunday services will be held in the EnginAer Hall, and Mr. Rich announced that at these services the experiment was to be tried of experiment as to be tried of illustrating the sermons by means of lantern views.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S,A,
div.p: Wycliffe P.S,A,

There was a very good meeting of this Society on Sunday. The Secretary presided, and spoke upon the "Goodness and mercy of God." He suggested happy thoughts of the goodness of God, as was evidenced in the seasons of the ear, in the home, and in the nation. He also touched upon the good- ness to the world by the higher intellects of the past as well as the present; the goodness of God in His great gift of His Son Jesus Christ; and God's merci- ful dealings with us, on -account of our weaknesses and sins as well as our failings. Mr. E. L. Jones gave the address upon "The sowing of the dead seed," showing that the seed must die to bring forth life. Christ died but rose again in newness of life and power.. God expected gifts from our higher life, seeds of kindness and service, and the best seed of a consecrated life, which should bring forth abundantly in useful lives, kindly people and willing and constant ! service. Miss J. Armstrong sang with good effect, I " 0 Divine Redeemer," which ei as greatly enjoyed, ; Mr. C. Cotton and Mr. A. }Raley also took part in the ! meeting, Mr. Payton, Miss. Bac., presided at the organ,and the members received their prize lists for the present half year. The happy meeting was brought to a close by singing "My God is reconciled," which Iwas most heartily joined in.

div.head: IMPERIAL AND NATIONAL DEFENCE.
div.p: IMPERIAL AND NATIONAL DEFENCE.
LETTER FROM Mg. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P.

We received yesterday, for publication, the following important letter on the much-discussed question of National and Imperial Defence, which Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., has addrqssed to Mr. J. Morton, the hon. secretary of the Warrington Progressive Labour League :-- Dear Mr. Morton,—l had intended referring in the course of my speech last Saturday evening, to some of the controversial questions connected with THE GREAT PROBLEM OF NATIONAL AND IMPERIAL DEFENCE which have recently given rise to so much dis- cussion in the press and in the country. But when I reached my notes on what I had intended to say on this topic I had already occu- pied so much of the time of the meeting, that having regard to the many attractive items on our programme, I felt it would be altogether unfair to trespass on the patience and indulgence of the ladies present as well as of our friends of the League by entering into a subject which one really could not discuss in very brief compass. I am not going to trespass on your time either, my friend, by attempting to enter in any sense exhaustively in this letter into a great and com- plex problem. But perhaps at this juncture when the very serious questions connected with this problem are occupying the minds of every- one here—certainly of everyone in the Liberal party, but I think I may say of everyone in the House without exception—and while it is an open secret that they have formed the subject of very prolonged consideration and debate in the Cabinet itself, I should like with your kind as- sistance to offer to our friends of the League and to yourself a few observations on the present satiation.

Well, then to begin with, it may have struck you as. it struck me as rather strange that the necessary increase in Naval Estimates was mentioned in the King's Speech some weeks before the responsible Minister, Mr. McKenna, would be in a position to explain and prove the necessity for this increase. But I am told on very good authority that there was a reason for this statement in advance in the King's Speech. That an increase in the Naval Estimates was in the present situation inevitable is generally admitted. Where the difference of opinion, and, indeed, sharp controversy has arisen has been, of course, on the all-important question "How much shall that iocrease be ?"- To a very large extent in a matter of this kind a Minister and a Parliament must look to experts for infofmation and advice. On the other hand, large issues of policy arise; political issues I mean, for g decision on which Parliament, and of course especially the Party in power must ultimately accept the responsibility. May I take this opportunity to say a word or two then on some of these issues?
In any scheme of: National and Imperia Defence

div.head: NAVY
div.p: THE NAVY

is naturally our first and foremost consideration. We are all familiar with the so-called two-power standard, and all, I think, equally agreed that we must maintain this as an irreducible mini- mum. The phrase as hitherto interpreted—at any rate by most of us—has hitherto meant that our Navy shall be equal to the next two strongest navies in Europe, plus 10% in our favour besides. Well, at the present time we are in that position with a very comfortable, and indeed I may say a very wide, margin of security in the shape of additional Naval strength beyond this into the bargain. I do not suppose that any of us will quarrel with that comfortable position. Very much the reverse. But if an attempt were made to lay it down as an axiom of policy in the future that however extensive a programme of Naval construction the United States may embark upon in the near future (I hope they will do nothing of the kind, but they may), and however ambitious the schemes of Naval construction on which Germany may embark even after 1912 is passed, we are to maintain our two-power standard plus 10% against these two countries with all their vast combined resources, I do not believe the country will approve of that; and I hope it will, not approve of this definition being construed as a Naval power fully equal to twice the Naval power of Germany. Taking all classes of ships into account, our marksmanship and seamanship, and the magnifi- cent persona of our voluntarily recruited Navy —taking all these things into consideration, we' have more than twice the strength of Germany on the water to-day, and. again I say that I do not suppose any of our friends will quarrel with that happy position of affairs. But when our friend the expert proposes to leave out of con- sideration all ships excepting those of the Dreadnought type, then I think it is wiser not to commit ourselves finally to any new interpreta- tion of the two-power standard which has hitherto served us and served us well.

div.head: MORE _DREADNOUGHTS.
div.p: MORE _DREADNOUGHTS.

It is reported in the Lobby this -evening that the question of futther construction of ships of the Dreadnought class has been compromised, those who wanted two and those who wanted six laying down this year, finally settling the question by deciding to lay down four. lam not .telling secrets, I simply send you a bit of Lobby gossip for what it may be worth. May I now for a moment before concluding this letter glance at the question of •

OUR LAND FORCES. In the opinion of most competent Judges our voluntary system assists us in recruiting our regular Army for service overseas. For my part, I have never felt that we could indulge in the luxury of a large regula: Army. It is only necessary for us to maintain, and therefore we only ought to maintain a small one which should be well-paid, well-equipped and thoroughly efficient, and which, if ever the necessity arose, would be augmented from the ranks of the Territorials. Content as I think we should be with a small regular Army, I feel very strongly that the Territorial Army for Home Defence will be an invaluable factor in providing for us all that national security which any rational being can desire. Such a force protects us against any trifling raids with which in time of war we might be harassed, and against which the Navy can never be a means of protection. It will also serve to protect us against invasion on a larger scale, and therefore, if the unExpected— the happily altogether improbable—should arrive, it will leave our Navy unshackled and free to strike wherever it is needed. I am, therefore, very glad-to hear that recruits for the Territorials are cnming in and coming in well, and I earnestly hope that both employers and employed in Lancashire will play a foremost part in helping to make a real success of this great scheme of Home Defence.
MR. HALDANE'S SCHEME VERSUS COMPULSORY SERVICE

A few days since there was a meeting in Lon- don of a large number of employers of labour who, as I understand, agreedi to give their em- ployes 21 days' holidays n the year with regular pay provided that of this time 14 days was de- voted to military service with the Territorials. That is the kind of support which I earnestly hope Mr. Haldane's scheme may receive through- out the country. If people in all ranks of life will only respond in that fashion there need be no fear for the success of Mr. Haldarre's under- taking, and when it is a success I am sanguine that most of those who have urged a compulsory plan, even though they may still think that plan preferable, will be glad that what is after all their chief object—reasonable national security—, has been attained: I daresay you will have noticed the action taken by the Alliance Insur- ance. Company whereby no man is allowed to enter their service unless he first serves with the Territorials. Personally, I should be very sorry to see employers, as a whole, in this country laying down a condition of that kind, the conse- quence of which would be obvious. Service with the Territorials, whether as an officer or in the ranks, may well count, and ought to count, in a man's favour. All honour to those who do serve and who, let ui be very certain, will have paid to them the honour which is their due, not ; only from the men but—more important still— from the women of England. But however

strongly we may hold this view don't let us lose our sense of proportion and talk as if military service were the one great service a man should render to his country. Men and women who give up their whole time to education, to the relief of the poor and unfortunate, to ambulance work, to sanitation and to a vast deal of other work voluntarily undertaken in this country, may render just as patriotic service even if they get less praise for it than those who arc cut out by temperament, circumstances; and general qualifications for military service. In this letter I have referred in a cursory manner to the military side of the question with which we are faced here, and however hateful the constant increase of expenditure on arma mcnts may be, we are bound to face it, and I for one have full confidence in the capacity of the present Government to judge of and to adopt the wise mean between such a reduction in our Naval and Military strength as compared with other nations as might some day prove a tempta- tion to some ambitious and utterly reckless statesman abroad, and on the other such an addition to the total fighting force of the Crown as would be regarded abroad as a menace tend- ing therefore to the formation of hostile com- binations against us. THE PRESENT INCREASE IN NAVAL ESTIMATES is caused by the action of Germany, and Germany alone. With her great over-sea com- merce it is only natural she should have a strong Navy, and she is committed to her programme till 1912. The great question is will she after that time continue to force the pace, and shall we then follow suit in this mad race of arma- ments. How is it to be stopped? By a better understanding between the democracies of the two nations. Yes, a rapprochement, and a better understanding between people in England and Germany. To that we must look forward, and I am convinced it is by that alone that in future years this, in every sense, wicked waste of the resourcct of two great nations will be stopped. • Will you kindly show this letter to the Presi- dent and the Executive of the League, and if you see fit to take steps to make it known to all the members of the League you are very welcome to do so. I must apologise for the inordinate length of this letter, but the whole question, as we know, not only of the utmost importance but also many-sided and far reaching. With best rrgarcis hrlL:ve me always, Very faithfully yours, A. H. CROSFIELD. Feb. 25th, 1909. P.S.—lt is reported from several quarters in the home counties that recruiting for the Territorials is going on apace, and is satisfactory not only in regard to numbers but also in regard to the first-rate class of men who are joining. As an illustration I hearon good authority that the Engineers will out-rival even if they don't outstriN in capacity the Engineers of the regular forces of the Line. This is splendid news and I for one firmly believe that in the long run it will tend towards a reduction of our total Naval and Military expenditure.

• DEATH OF MR. JOHN DUN. _ A Successful Banker.. Many 'Warrington people will deeply regret to hear": of the death of Mr. John Dun, formerly general manager of Parr's' Bank, Limited, and latterly a director, who passed away at his residence, Waising- , ham, Chislehurst, on Sunday. It is many years since • Mr. Dun severed his connection with this district but he never ceased to hold a warm place in the regard of a large circle of IVarringCn friends. De was one of the most prominent figures in the world of banking, and possessed a magnetic personality in which_ shrewdness, pushfuluess and sagacity, as well as- kindliness and geniality of manner all had their part.:, He was born in Edinburgh in 1833 and after a distinguished school career he entered tho Bank: of Scotland where his progress was remarkable... When only thiity years of age ho had attained tho'. position of chief inspector in the Bank and his reputa— tion at that time (1864) was such as to cause the directors of Parr's Bank in the following year to con- gratulate themselves that they had secured his services as manager and secretary. Parr's Bank then was a comparatively small provincial institution with head offices at Warrington, with only three branches and a deposit account of £909,870. At that time the late Mr. Thomas .Parr, of Grappenhall Heyes, was chairman and the directors included Lord Cross. When. Mr. Dun retired from the position of manager, in 1902, it had, by virture of his progressive policy,grown to a bank of national importance, with 140 branches and sub-branches and a deposit account of .7£24,510,644 Up to seven years ago he made the chief history of Parr's Bank, and after his retirement as manager and until his death, he was a director. Not many years ago, at the annual meeting of the cciarpany, held at the Cannon-street Hotel, London, Mr. Dun was pre- sented with £lO,OOO in recognition of his services. He compiled a well-known book on bank statistics, was a member of the Executive and Council of the Institute of Bankers, and of the Association of English Country Bankers. Be was a linguist and diligent student of literature. In 1893, consequent upon the growth of the London business of the bank,he went to live at Walsingliam, Chislehurst During the many years that Mr. Dun was associated with the bank at Warrington he did much useful public work. He was a great lover of music and took consider- able interest in the Warrington Musical Society.lle was a member of the Literary and Philosophical Society and read papers on a variety of subjects at the meetings of that organization. A staunch Churchman, Mr. Dun was a _regular attender at Christ Church, Latchford. In politics his sympathies were with the Unionists. Mr. Dun was an ardeirtfrgolfer, and to him and a few others the foundation of the Royal Liverpool Golf Club at Hoylake was due. In 1868 he and a handful of friends of like bent played on the now classic links before the course was made. They were impressed with tbe possibilities of the land, and in 1869 he assisted in starting the world-famed Royal Liverpool Club, which has tinned out so many golfers of the first rank.

Mr. Dun married in 1861 Eliza, daughter of Mr John Marrison, of Edinburgh, and she died at Chisl- hurst on August Ist, 1900. He married again in autumn of of 1907, his wife being Annie, widow of th •:: Rev. Richard Pearson, and she died in March, 1908 The surviving children are Mr. Finlay Dun (a partner': in the firm of Messrs. Gill, Archer, Maples and Dun solicitors, Liverpool), Mr. J. Arthur Dun, Mr. Robert , Dun (now at Kartoum as Advocate-General to the Soudanese (overnment), and Mrs. Edelsten (wife of _ Colonel Edelsten, secretary of the West Lancashire Division Territorial Force) ; also Miss Laura Pearson, . a step-daughter. THE FUNERAL. The funeral took place on Thursday at Chislohnrst, Kent. The vicar of the Parish Church, the Rev. James E. Dawson, officiated. The members of the family present included Mr. Finlay Dun (eldest son). and M. s. Finlay Dun (daughter-iu-law), Mr. Arthur Dun (eon), Mrs. Edelsten (daughter) and Colonel Edelsten (son-in- law), the Rev. James Dun (brother), Mits E. C. Dun (niece), Mrs. H. Dalton (niece), and Mr. H. Dalton, MT. (reramt rert3li reoo.i.), and Miss Pearson. Among others who attended the funeral were Mr. Cecil F. Parr (chairman Parr's Bank), Mr. A. J. Fraser (deputy-chairman Parr's Bank), Mr. R. W. Whalley (general manager Parr's Bank), Mr. W. D. Hughes (of the Liverpool branch of the bank), Mr. Gourlay (of the Bank of bcotland, with which the late Mr. Dun was at one time connected), Mr. John Murray (late secretary Parr's Bank branch at Warrington.) Widnes, of which borough Mr. Dun was for many years treasurer, was represented by the Mayor (Councillor Smith) and Alderman Owens (chairman of the Finance Committee). Others present included Mr. A. Travers Hawess, J.P., - Mr. Ford, Miss Ford, Mr. Steele, and Mr. John Margetson. The wreaths sent numbered about thirty. Besides those sent by Mr. Dun's family and the household servants, there were wreaths from the head office of Parr's Bank, London, and the Warrington branch staff.

Most of the members present gave their views on the subject, nearly all being opposed to Mr. Newton.

Councillor Broadhurst's Onemployed Bill

After the great effort of last week many members of our local Parliament apparently thought they we*e entitled to a rest from their labours on Tuesday even- ing, and there was a considerable falling off in the attendance. The topic for discussion was a Bill intro- duced by Councillor James Broadhurst (President of the Local Government Board) "to provide employment for the unemployed by establithing productive State Industries which will not enter into unnecessary competition with existing industries." The provisions of the measure are :- 1. (a) That a permanent , Government department denominated the National Employment Board shall he constituted, composed of two representatives nominated by each of the following bodies :—The Board of Trade, the Commissioners of Woods and Forests, the Board of Agriculture, the Lecal Govern_ rnent Board, the Home Office, and the Federation of Trade Unions. 1. (b) That this department shall he represented in Parliament by a Minister of Cabinet Rank. 2. That full compulsory powers be granted to the Board to purchase land in any part of the United Kingdom for the purposes of Afforestation, Preven- tion of "Cc set Erosion, or any Works of Public Utility.. 3. That the Board commence forthwith the Afforesta- , • tion of the 9,000,000 acres of land, suitable for that purpose, at the rate of 150,001 acres per year. 4. That tbe SUM of £2,000,000 per annum, necessary to develop this scheme, shall be raised by a loan, the interest on which shall be paid out of the public revenues. 5. That the workmen, employed by the Board shall receive the rate of pay per hour recognized as the Standard for similar work in the district. 6. That any; person employed by the Board shall (if he request) be granted permission to absent himself a reasonable length of time, for the purpose of seeking permanent employment elsewhere. 7. That this Bill shall not deprive any Authority of any Power which it may now possess. 8. That Distress Committee, Labour Bureaux, Boards of Guardians, end ell similar bodies, using the powers given them under the Unemployment Act of 1905, shell co-operate with the Board in assisting applicants to find suitable employment. '9. That Clause 53 in the Kefoem Act of 183'2 (which , provides that no person shall be entitled to ha registered as an elector who shall have, within 12 Calendar months, received Parochial Relief) shall not apply to persons employed by virtue of the powers contained in this Act. Councillor BROADITURST, in submitting the Bill, said that according to a return issued by the Federation of Trades [Thiene the number of unemployed in this country was estimated at 1,500,000. Such a state of things, he believed, did not exist ie any other country in the world. Detending his inclusion of the Federation of Trades Unions in the organizations represented in the •d ,rttnent. ee said he did _not consider that the

new depa. Labnur Representation Commit-tee represented the feelings of the trade unionists of the country t tsh member of a legal trade union generally contributed a half-penny week to the Federation and there was no political party attached to it. At the present time he was sorry to eay the Labour Representation Committee was totally composed of the Socialist party of Great Britain. (Cordial " hear,hea.r " from Nlts, Nightingale). Referring to the proposed representation of the Depart- ment by a Minister of Cabinet rank, Councillor Broad- hurst said that was the direct wish of the Conference of the Labour Party, and the Government were only too pleased to try and meet the desires of Labour. As to the compulsory purchase of land, the House, and ' more especially the Socialist party, would agree that it was desirable to obtain this employment for the workingman end we should also have something to fall back upon in the future, instead of depending tolely upon foreign powers to provide us with our raw material for building operations or similar work. (Laughter.) Allwling to the rate of pay to workers in the State industries, Councillor Broadherst remarked : "As a strone trade unionist and a member who has risen to a position of £2,00 a year—(laughter)-4 don't forget the class I formerly belonged to, and I am of opinion that wherever a man is employed, he should receive the standard and the trsde union rate of the dis- trict." Uh fortunately in the past when an unemployed workman had had to seek assistance from the Guardians he had been disfranchised and lost his citizenship. That was a downright shame, and there would be no such disability imposed on those who worked in the State industries. (Applause). M. F. A. JENKINS (Postmaster General) formally seconded the adoption of the Bill. 'ATI-. J. A. J. NIOISTON (L , Battersea) said he could not congratulate the President of the Local Government Board on the substance of the measure. The constitu- tion of the new department would not be on demo- cratic lines and there were pieces of co-optation to which many Liberals would strongly object. The President of the Local Government Board himself admitted that the inclusion of the Federation of Trade Unions was likely to " dish " the the, (Councillor Broadhurst : "No, no "). The granting of com- pulsory powers for land purchase was the main innova- tion of the Bill. It. could not be claimed that the measure was a cure for unemployment. As a matter of fact neither afforestation, reclamation of fore-shores nor works of public utility could have that effect. If nfforestation were carried on by capitalists for profit no-one would claim that it would do anything even to palliate the unemployed problem, and the economic effects if the undertaking were a Government one would be just the same. Afforestation would take up a very small percentage of the nnernployed—in fact it woelcl scarcely touch the fringe of the question. As to reclamation of fore-shores, there was the same objection that We would not see the result for many years and in the meantime the taxpayers would be taxed to provide the wages, and the effective purchasing power of the people would be redaced," and there would ha a tendencY to lower wages generally. The schemes would, therefore. in the long run tend to the detriment of the people. The rate of wages t 6 be paid was very indefieite. There was not afforestation or reclamation of fore-shores in every district, so that where the standard rate came in it was difficult to see. ',ant the people wanted was not trees or the reclamation of fore-shores, but food, cloth- ing and the necessities of life and it was upon such industries that they should be directly or indirectly employed. He did not see how the Government seharne, without altering the basis of our indus- trial system. was going to affect the problem one iota. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, Mr. T. S. Steel applied for temporary authority to be granted to Air. C. W. Corbett, ButtermArket-street to sell at the Lower Angel in the place of Ilr. William Osborne.— The application was granted. Son to Lord and Lady Acton. _

The" Times announce-the birth of a son to Lord and Lady Acton. Lord Acton is in the diplonttic service, and has been in attendance on tlie King. His wife was Miss Lyon, daughter of Mr. T. H. Lyon, of Appleton Hal!, Warrington. Howley Athletic A.F C.

The members of this club held their annuli dance in the Assembly loom of ale Conservative Club, Sankey-street and the affair 'droved a great success. Dancing commenced at eight o'clock, and was con- tinued with zest until two a.m. The M.C.'s were Messrs. C. Smart and W. Warburton.
BA.RGATNS in Silver-plated Teapots, Cruets, Pre- serve Dishes, etc.. during Sale.—J. S. GARIAND, 51, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Elective Auditors.

Messrs. Ebenezer England and Llurence Bolton have been returned unopposed as elective auditors for the borough. We, published the names of Mr. England's nominators last week. Mr. Bolton, accountant, was proposed by the Rev. E. C. E Carleton, seconded by Mr. T. A. Salton, and supported by Messrs. W. W. Leigh, F. W. Ward, A. S. Wright, P. G. Cooke, T. A. Ashcroft, Richard Bailey, James Gleave and Thomas Nixon.

Mrs Booth Sings at a Manchester Concert. Mrs. Arthur Booth, of Warrington, appeared as'a soloist on Saturday evening at the promenade concert in connection with the Manchester Orchestras Limited, at the Free Trade Hall. She gave a fine interpreta- tion of Leoncavallo's Ballatella (" Pagliacci ") and Weber's recit and aria "Softly sighs " (Der Frieschutz). A. Manchester contemporary iu its critique of the concert says :—" it is a matter of regret that this clever soprano is not heard oftener in the North."

About 60 members and friends assembled at the Museum on Monday evening to hear a lecture on " Old Warrington," by Mr. Charles gadeley, curator and librarian. The lecture was given in one of the rooms upstais, which contains most of Warrington's antiquities. Mr. Afadeley possesses a rare fund of infoanation and he made his subject thoroughly interesting. There were on view some very old and valuable documents which are in the possession of the Museum At the close the Rev. John Yonge moved a hearty vote of thaoks to gr. gadeley, which was seconded by Ur. J. Monks and carried. Dog Exemption Licences Refused.

At the Borough Police Court on Tuesday Joseph Shaw, a herdsman, applied for exemption from obtain- ing a licence for his dg. He said the dog was not his own but belonged to his employers. The Deputy Town Clerk (fr. Holloway) opposed the exemption and the application was refused. —Thomas Chadwick, a farm bailiff, employed at the Training College, also asked for an exemption. The Clerk : Is it your dog? The Applicant,: No, it is practically nobody's. The Chief Constable: Oh ! I will sefad a constable round there to take charge of a stray dog. The application was refused Military Funeral.

With -full military 11-moire the funeral took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Sunday of the late Private J. Massey, D. Co. of the 4th battalion, South Lancashire Regiment. The deceased, who died at the Infirmary from an internal complaint, had been con- nected with the old Volunteer corps for 25 years, and with the Territorial Force since it was formed. A large contingent of Territorials, including a firing party under the direction of Sergeant Morris, paracnd at the Drill Hall at 1.30 and broceeded to Baxter- street, the late residence Of the demased, where they were joined by the mourners. On the way to the Cemetery the regimental band under the direction of Bandmaster Richardson, played the Dead March in " Saul " and "The vacant chair." The escort was under the direction of Captain C L. Williamson. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton LINSEED CONIPOUND 'for Coughs and Gilds. Of proven efficacy.
