Mr. Wolmersley presided at the eighth meeting of the winter session, ancliglir. W. Burton, of L.)wton, son of Alderman Burton, lectured on" The vegetation of Sand Dunes." lie dealt with the botany of the Dunes in the neighbourhood of Scuthport,which he had care- fully studied during a residence of several years in that locality and showed how certain plants had adapted themselves by morligcations in the growth of stem, leaf and flower, to the special conditions of the locality, and, in particular, there was an animated discussion. A feature of the evening's proceedings was the acknowledgement, by special vote of thinks, of the generosity of Mr. Charles White, who has been actively associated with the club from its inception, and who has presented to it an excellent microscope, to be kept at the Museum, and to be available for any menn'ber engaged in microscopic work.

PUBLIC BENEE;IT UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHERE.—Advt. Hatton Show. The annual meeting of the workers in connection with this popular horicultural show was held in the Parish Rolm on Frid ty evening, when the President (the Rev. T. T. Lee-Jones) presided over an excellent attendance. The Secretary (Mr. J. G. Hatton) pro- duced the baldric° sheet showing a balance in the bank to the society's credit of £5O 17s. 101., which was considered highly satisfactory. The Ron and Rev. C. F. Cross was elected president, the Rev. T. T. Lee-Jones and gr. James Parr, vice-presidents,Messrs R. L. Warburton and John Done, chairman and vice- chairman of the Committee of Management, Mr. James Parr and Mr. R. L. Warburton, trustees, and Mr. J. G. Hatton, secretary. Several alterations in the prize list were agreed upon, and a suggestion thitt an exhibition of poultry be included in the next show met with a cordial recePtion. The following were appointed to consider the proposal : —Messrs. J. Wright, Thomas Ditchfield, Isaac Hewitt, Richard Billington, R. L. Warburton and H. Bannister.
PUBLIC BENEFIT.-TINDER, THE cLopfc FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. A Biblical Play. _ _

At St. George's Mission on Saturday a short Biblical play entitled "Scenes from the Life of Joseph," written for the girls of the afternoon Mission by the Curate-in-charge (the Rev. T. A. J. Ridpa.th) was preSented for the first time before a large audience. The girls had been trained by Miss A. Buckley and other ladies, and incidental music was given by Miss Mary Gornall, Miss Gladys Stewart, Miss Clarice Newall, Mrs. Reynolds, Mrs. H. Waring, Miss Reynolds and Miss Fairclough The scenery was the handiwork and gift of three members of the Mission Mr. James Frangleton, Mr. A. Clare,. and Mr. J. Kenwright. The stage managers were Mr. Kenwright and Sergeant Hinton, Miss Sarah Darby- shire took the part of Jacob, and her acting was very creditable. Miss Hannah Allen (Joseph); Miss Nellie Healer (Judah), and the steward of Joseph's 'house- hold (Miss Lucy Hill), all did exceptionally well. The play, which was again peformed on Thursday, is admirably written and reflects great credit upon its author.

The Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson delivered a Lecture on this topic under the auspices of the Liver- pool Garden City Association, at the Common Hall, Hackins-hey, Liverpool. _He sketched the conditions of the ideal city beautiful, in which all citizens, rich and poor, lived together. In our cities, he said, no attempt was made at- arrangement. They welcomed the Liverp:ol Bill, and looked forward with hope to Mr. John Barn's Town Planning Bill as a step in the right direction, and hoped the measure would not be made a contentious one. In Warrington the first difficulty they had was the builder, who, although there were rnany applications, did not come forward to build the houses, but preferred to continue erecting rows of cottages in the streets. The second difficulty was the Co operative Society, which did not come fcrward as one hoped they would have done, and they had not got the response ,from the working men they wished and hoped for. The project however, was goilfg‘on, but not with that rapidity he hoped it would do. If the movement xvaS to be a real movement it must not be a philanthropic thing. They wanted to see the working men doing the thing for themselves, and thus only would they get the real interest which would Make the scheme a success.

A well-attendecl sacred concert was given in the Palace and Hippodrome on Sunday evening in which. the playing of Crosfield's Brass Band was the principal feature. The fine body of instrumentalists comprising the band performed some pieces new and old under Mr. Halliwell's conductorship in a manner which fully sustained the high position they have attained in brass band circles within quite a recent period. Not only was there nicely balanced and full-toned ensemble playing. " Crosfield's "includes soloists df conspicuous ability, and in work of this kind for the cornet,- tenor hbrn, euphonium or trombone, we doubt whether any organisation in the neighburhood can put forward better and more artistic executants. There were passages presenting formidable difficulties of phrasing and technique in b ,th the "II Trovatore " and the " Maritana " selections, in the surmounting of which the various solo players seemed to take a real pleasure, while in the more massive portions of these pieces the tone volume and *the precision was really. admirable. The audience shewed their high appreciation of these good things-by frequent and enthusiastic applause. The vocalist Madame Lena Mitchell scarcely brought out fully the potentialities of "The Enchantress." While the intonation and enunciation were by no means bad, Madame Mitchell's interpretation lacked expression and any approach to dramatic intensity and it therefore failed to move and convince N.:r did we care for the long drawn out rendering of " Annie Laurie" as to which it would be difficult to " enthuse" under the best of circumstances. Miss Clarice Newall played the pianoforte accom- paniments tastefully but much too quietly to be effective. _
We understand that towards the close of the Lenten interval Crosfield's band will give a further concert with the deserving object of beneitting our local nursing institution.

div.p: The Women's Circle.

The advance made by the Women's Circle in War- rington was abundantly proved at the "Pancake Social "held at the Liberal Club on Tuesday night. The one drawback was that the rooms were so packed out that only the early arrivals enjoyed the excellent programme in comfort. Mrs. Smethurst presided, supported by HAL Willett, Miss Gomel', Mrs. Dunn, and other ladies interested. The two speeches of the evening were made by the President Mrs. Dodds and Miss Bessie Dutton, whose words were both sweet and serious. Mrs. Dodds Presented the following prizes for the December competitions: Cakee,Miss Plinston, and Miss P. Heywood ; dolls, Miss Boardman, Misses lace and Dever. best shilling article, Mrs. Hawthorn, Misses \laud Jones and Maggie Heywood; pinafores, handmad, Nellie Barnett ; • machine, Miss Bell, Agnes Freeman ; small extras Mrs. Davies and Mrs. Littlevvood. The prizes fr the ponnds of most intrinsic value belonged to Mrs. Wright and Miss Ruth Balmford. The collector of the largest number of pounds was Mrs. Heywood The prize for the best paper read at the Circle on December 31st was presented to Miss Polly Heywood and a small book ;(3 Miss Annie Roberts, Mrs. Dodds , then presented to MK Letheren ! a• beautiful silver inkstand inscribed, and a pair of gold studs. The value of the gift from the members was enhanced by the gracious way in which it was given. Mrs. Jackson Holmes presided at the piano throughout the evening( She opened with a piano , solo, arranged a cempetitien—" Musical Snatches" (prize, Miss May Tynan) and accompanied the artistes.' I Mrs. Peart and Miss Mani Hipkiss were the soloists; recitations were given by Miss Gertrude Henshall, and Miss Truslove, and mandoline solos by Miss Dorothy Turner; a duet " The gipsy maid" by the Misses Hamer in costume. Another competition was arranged by Miss Marsh guessing the contents of different cards (prize Miss Nancy na rker). The refreshments reflected great credit on the.Cornmittee. The pancakes made by Mesdames Starkey, Heywood, Elwell, Patrick and Pepper, came up light, plentiful and "red hot." , Mrs. Holmes announced the clotsing concert of the first session for April 17th in Bold-street Schoolroom.
AS NECESSMrZY AS THE COOK.
"Currants," says a modern writer on culinary

matters," are now almost as necesstiry as the cook." We have, indeed,become so appreciative of these homely little berries, that no menu is to be conside,rad quite complete without them. Currant sauce is, in some families taking the place of apple sauce, and is found to be a very welcome change, especially at this season of the year, when apples are so lacking in flavour and when dried currants are in their very best condition. One must never forget that this favourite fruit is not only tempting to the appetite, but really splendid for the health. Their is an extraordinary amount of true nourishment packed up within each tiny little berry and for this reason both adults and children should ea freely of this wholesome fruit.
UNCLE NED.
HOW TO MAKE PEOPLE HAPPY.

DEAR UNCLE NED,—If we want to make those peop!e happy whom we come in contact with we must strive to be _thoughtful, sincere, obedient, unselfish, agreeable, and considerate. In the first place, it is our duty and privilege to endeavour to make our parents happy by willing obedience to their wishes, to give them our best love, to help them to the best of our abilities, and to sympathise with them in their troubles. When our !no-thus are sick and weary, then a splendid opportunity is presented to us to make her happy and cheerful by doing all that lies ia our. power to make her burden lighter. Our fathers are made happy by watching our efforts to please mother. To our brothers and -sisters we should be loving .and kind, sharing alike their joys and sorrows, that their lives may be made brighter and happier. Our teachers- in the day schools and Sunday schools can be made happy by our paying strict attention to the lessons that they wish us to learn, and by letting them see that we are better children for all the trouble they have gone through to -make us proficient and good. There rue .-splendid opportunities presented to us amongst the poor; if e -know of a poor child who is sick in bed we can take some 'nourishing food and a few flowees, and we shall be amply repaid by the look of happiness that will be shown on the child's face. To the' aged people we should always be gentle and kind, and treat them with the utmost it-spect. Tiiere is a nretty story told of our late Queen Victoria', which is as 101.1013.'S :-111 the village close to Balmoral Castle there lived a very poor, but pieus, old Scotchwoman, Wir.os3 delight it was to read a portion of the Scriptures every day, but as she got older her eyes began to fail her, and she could not manage to read at all. Now our late ;Queen was known to vi•ii the old lad very often, when she was staving in the High- lands, and read/the Bible to her, and in several other ways made the old womm's laiteridays brighter and happier. We cannot all do the good acts that our. late Queen did, but if ever we have the chance to make other people happy we should avail ourseiv,s of the opportunity. ---c-
WILLIAM B. FmtnAß
MAKING OTHERS HAPPY.

My idea is to make slums happy. The very word slum brings 'before us a sune of po\-erty, of half-starved, pale-faced children. They are brought up roughly, and without t ducation they live in bad ventilated mints, using one room for' sittinc,:room, bedroom, and kitchen. The home is where the first lessons of citizen- ship are learnt. Just think of the chi dren being brought up in such homes. 'lt seems impossible that children can be happy hi such homes, Yet, strange, to say,- the slum-dweller soon finds gladness. We often see them singing and dancing to the strains of the street-org,m. These poor children could soon be made happy by giving them a good tea and presents. No one knows how happy the little slum child is if he thinks he is going out to tea. He is so happy that he can scarcely sleep. They are dressed in their poor clothes, faces washed. and hair brushed, and then the child is ready for going. The slum children nre.so happy that they do not mind their ragged clothes, and when each is given a warm garment and an orange you would not find a happier chid than the poor slum, and you would feel happy because you have helped to make some one happy. " Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of these My brethren, ye have done it unto Me."

div.head: HE ASSISTED THE MAGISTRATE.
div.p: HE ASSISTED THE MAGISTRATE.

A prominent pollee-court magistrate-, passing one d':y throng!' the City, and not. being pressed for time. availed himself of the outside of an omn!ip.ls instead of patronizing the more arist,ocratle cab.

" All fares, lease!"p came the familiar cry, when, ti-xusting his hand into his pocket, the ornament of the magisterial Bench d:scovered, to his consternation, that he had come out without a farthing of money. An explanation of the state of . affairs was proceeding, and being taken in very 111 part by the conductor, when a man, sitting near, suddenly pulled out two pennies from his Waistcoat-pocket, and said : I'll pay for yer." The ticket was duly punched and handed over, whereupon the gentleman, moving nearer his benefactor, said:—

div.head: POSTAL AND SAVINGS BANK REGULATIONS RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: POSTAL AND SAVINGS BANK REGULATIONS RUGBY FOOTBALL.
For further particulars see "Post Qffice Guide," at any Post Office. POSTAGE STAMPS._ _
Books containing 12 penny and 23 halfpenny stamps are now on sale at each post office. Price 2s.
INLAND CORR.ESPONDENC E.

The term " Correspondence" means cor- respondence posted within the United Kingdom, including the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands. "Inland Correspondence" is divided into the following classes: (a) Letters (b) Postcards (c) halfpenny packets Not only letters, but any document or article (with a few trifling exceptions) which can be trans- mitted by post at all, may be sent by letter post, the only limitation being that of size. LETTER POST. The prepaid rate of postage is as follows : Not exceeding 4 ozs. in weight ... ld. For every additional 2 0z5.... id. A letter posted unpaid is chargeable on delivery with double postage; a letter insufficiently paid, with double the deficiency. No letter may exceed two feet in length, one foot in width, or one foot in depth. POST-CARDS.
(d) Newspapers (e) Parcels

The prepaid rate of postage on every post-card is one half-penny, anti on every reply post-card one penny. A post-card posted unpaid is chargeable oa delivery with one penny. Cards used as post-cards must be made of ordinary card-board, not thicker than the material used for the thickest official post-card. They may not exceed 51 inches in length by 3i incites in width, or he less than 3/ inches in length by 2/ inches in width. A gummed label (not to exceed 2 inches long and ;7-inch wide) bearing the address may now be affixed to the address side of card. If any of the rules relating to a post-card be infringed, the card will be treated as a letter.

HALFPENNY PACKET POST. The Halfpenny Packet Post can be used only far packets not exceeding 2oz. in weight. Printed matter, &c., net in the nature of a letter, may be transmitted by this method. NEWSPAPER POST. The prepaid rate of postage on a registered news- paper, including any supplement thereto, whether posted singly or with others is id. Newspapers not registered at the General Post Office are treated in the post like any other printed matter.

PARCEL POST. The rates of postage on parcels areas follows: For a parcel ... ... not exceeding 1 lb. 0 3 ff exceeding 1 lb. )2 2 lb. 0 4 II 7) 2 lb. 9/ 3 lb. 0 5 PII 91 3 lb. )1 5 lb. 0 6 / f 9, 5 lb. n 7 lb. 0 7 t 1 ~7 lb. ff 8 lb. 0 8 If If 8 lb. n 9 lb. 0 9 If !I - 9 lb. ~ 10 lb. 010 f, fl 10 lb. ~ 11 lb. 011 No parcel may exceed 111 b. in weight. The size allowed for an inland parcel is : Greatest length... ... ... ... 3 ft. G in. Greatest length and girth combined 6 ft. 0 in. For example—A parcel measuring 3ft. 61n. in its longest dimensions as much as 2ft. 6in. round its thickest part; a short parcel may be thicker; thus, if it measure no more than 31t. in length, it may measure as much as 311. round its thickest part. The postage on a parcel must be prepaid. Mark each parcel" Parcel Pest." A parcel must not be posted in a letter box, but presented at the counter of a post office, and the sender should see that the weight, size and postage are in order before leaving.

PARCELS -(FORIIIGN AND COLONIAL). Parcels are accepted for parcel post to most foreign countries under conditions similar to the inland regulations, except that for customs require- ments the contents must be declared. T'e customs charges can be prepaid or collected on delivery. The postage varies to different countries and must be prepaid. Mosul' ORDERS (INLAND.) The postal authorities cannot issue a single money order for more than £4O, and will only cash them at the money order office at which they are made payable, unless they are crossed, when they can be paid through a bank. No fractional pait of a Id. can be contnined in a money order. The rates of poundage are :—Not exceeding 21, 2d. ; £3, 3d.; £lO, 4d.; £2O, 6d.; £3O, Bd. ; £4O, 10d. By paying an additional 2d. and cost of the telegram of advice, a money order can be telegraphed under certain restrictions. MONEY ORDERS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL.) The maximum amount for which a money order may be issued for places abroad varies in each particular place. The poundage rates are :—Not exceeding £1,3d.; £2, 6d. ; and above that, 3d. for each additional £2 or portion of it. A fee of 6d. in addition to the ordinary poundage, together with cost of telegram of advice, enables money orders to be telegraphed to certain places abroad.
Pus raz. -Orkamits.

These are obtainable at any money order office in the United Kingdom and possess the advantage over money orders that they can be cashed at any money 'order office. If crossed, they can be paid into a' bank. They are issued for fixed amounts, rising by 6d., from 6d. to £1 Is. The poundage fees are up to 2s. 6d.; Id. nil, to 155.; lid. up to 21s. Before parting with a postal order, always fill in the name of the person to whom the amount is to be paid. Each order is numbered, as is also the counterfoil attached, which latter should be retained and name of payee filled in. The Post- master-General will entertain no further claim after an order is once paid. Stamps to the amount of sd. can be affixed to make up odd sums: TELEGRAMS (INLAND).

The Postmaster-General possesses,almost entirety, the privilege of transmitting,collecting and deliver- ing telegrams in the United Kingdom. 'the charge for a telegram is a minimum amount of 6d.' which covers 12 words, and an additional id. for each extra word. This charge includes delivery within the postal district if sent out for delivery from a head telegraph office, but if from a sub-office then within three miles only, beyond which a charge of 3d. per mile is made from the office door. All charges are, as far as possible, prepared by affixing stamps to telegram form. Address of person receiv- ing a telegram has to be paid for, but sender's name if written on back of form need not he. Five figures count as one word. The cost of a reply may be prepaid. Telegrams can be repeated on payment of half the original charge, which extra payment is refunded if error is detected. Telegrams may be posted in wall or pillar boxes, or handed to rural postmen, and are wired as soon as received at the nearest telegraph office. Late fees secure attention, in certain cases, to telegrams handed in after the usual hours. The cost of registering an abbrevi- ated address, which must consist of two words, is £1 is. TELEGRAMS (FOREIGN AND COLONIAL) Must be written on special forms and are accepted in the language of any of the principal European countries. The rates vary, and are too numerous to detail here. POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK.

These arie-siablisi;ed at all money order offices. In ordinary cases the annual deposit must not exceed £5O, and the total amount £2OO. No person can have more than One account. Amounts placed in the bank on behalf of children under seven years of age cannot be withdrawn until the child reaches that age, and then only under his or her own signa- ture. The smallest amount received at a time is is., and this may take the form of 12 penny stamps affixed to a special form. Each depositor receives a bank book in which the amount of each deposit should be entered at the time of paying in. If the deposit is £1 or over, a special acknowledgment is sent from the head London office. Interest is allowed at the rate of 2i per cet.t. Any amouht up to and including RI may be withdrawn without previous notice, on presenting a bank book. The bank book should be sent each year, postage free, on the anniversary of the date when the account was opened, to the Controller of the Savings Bank Repartment for purposes of checking and adding interest. The withdrawal of money can be e xpedited by telegraphing, the depositor paying cost of telegrams.

Oldham's Revenge —Warrington Weil-Beaten.

Immense interest was taken in the return match between Warrington and Oldham on Saturday, seeing that Warrington were the first team to beat the Spinners and put on a record score of 27 points to nil at, Wilderspool. Beautiful weather favoured the return, and something like 500 supporters accompanied the Warrington men. Oldham had a tremendous backing owing to the interest taken in the fixture, and there were quite 23,000 spectators on the ground, which was in good order though devoid of grass. Oldham were absolutely at full strength, but Warrington had to make a last minute change which injured their chances. Taylor stood down owing to an injured leg, and Hockenball was drafted in the team for the first time for two years. The team were as follows : Oldham—Wood, back; Tyson, G. W. Smith, Llewellys and Oldershaw three-quarter backs ; Avery (captain) and Beynon, half backs ; Ferguson, A. Smith, Wright, Longworth, Wilkinson and Jardine, forwards. Warrington—Tilley,. back ; Treherne, Hockenhall, Dickenson (captain), end Fish, three-quarter backs; Brooks and Jenkins, half backs ; Neill, Dowell, Board- man, Tharnas, Belton and Shugars, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Priestley (Salford). Touch judges, Messrs. AV. Gregory (Runcorn) and W. T. Chapman (Swinton). Warrington won the toss, and Oldham started the great game by a punt to Hockenhall, which was badly returned and play settled in the Warrington half. ,Here there were some keen exchanges, but neither side com- bined well. Beynon went in for abort ground-kicking from the scrum and somewhat upset the Warrington I back division, so that when the bail was handled the ' men seemed out of place and A. Smith galloped over , after weak attempts to tackle him. The goal-kick failed and the Warrington forwards at once rushed the game ;to the other end, Woods return going into touch. ' Jenkins got the ball away to the left, but Dickenson's pass to Fish was snapped up by Tyson who ran half the length of the field before he was compelled to part by Brooks. The ball was sent over the Warrington line, but Tilley got up first and sent dead. While on the , defence Warrington were penalised and Wood kicked a I goal from an easy position. Warrington were beaten for possession, but O'Neill lead some fine dribbles, one of which took play right to the line, where Wood was collared and had to play the ball. O'Niell and Belton both made strenuous efforts to cross but were held a foot outside. There was a keen struggle here, and Warrington should have equalised when they got possession, but a shocking pass by Brooks went to the ground, and the ball was kicked clear. Half-time: Oldham, five points, Warrington nil. In resuming, the home side had the advantage of the breeze, and by good punting took play to the Warring- ton quarter. Avery was tacked in possession once when a pass would have sent Tyson over, but a moment later the ball went by way of Avery and Smith to Tyson who just grounded at the corner as Fish bowled him into touch in goal. It was a smart try, but the goal by Wood from the touch-line surpassed it and the cheering was loud and long. The scoring ought to have finished here, but a weak kick by Treharne gave Avery a a walk over near the posts, and Wood converted again. Warrington played up pluckily, though they showed littlo of their customary. con- fidence. Dickenson made a fine run, hut held the ball too long and was pulled down by Smith, when Fish was waiting for the pass. Another good forward rush took play once more to the line, and here Warrington would have scored, had luck been on their side. The ball rebounded from an Oldham defender right into Wood's hands, and was immediately punted to centre. Smith and Tyson took play to the Warrington half, and Avery getting hold after a clear knock on scored a simple try without Wog challenged. In the last five minutes, IBrooks ran nearly the length of the field and passed to 'Hockenhall,.who made a tricky effort to get through, and was tackled near the line. Final : Oldham, 3 goals. 4 tries, 18 points ; Warrington, nil.

div.head: RUNCORN v. WIGAN: THE LEADERS WIN.
div.p: RUNCORN v. WIGAN: THE LEADERS WIN.

At Runcorn, before nearly 7,090 spectators. The start was sensational, the ball being taken well into the visitors' half, where Butterworth put in a fine kick, which wus followed by Moran running up and scoring. Jolley failed at goal. Jones and Thonias forced Runcorn back, and Thomas got possession from the pack and scored, for Ley them ,to add a capital goal. The ball travelled from enl to end, and a round of passing between Jones, Thomas and Miller ended in r line try by the last-named, Leytham adding a goal. Butter- worth and Flanagan soon got to the Wigan line, where Watton rnarkeh. Jolley's shot at goal fell outside, but Flanagan, who had smartly followed rip,safely grounded the ball. Jolley failed at goal. Half-time : Wigan, 2 goals 2 tries (10 points).; Runcorn, 2 tries (6 points). After the interval Wigan were fora short time forced to defend. From a penalty. kick Jolley landed a goal. Thomas, Jenkins, and Leytham made strenuous efforts to get through, without success. Leythani then placed a goal from a n:Esk. Keen play followed, and Watton sadly. mulled the ball, leaving Jenkins to pick up the score, Leytharnimproving. A brilliant round of passing between Jolley, Watton and Butterworth, Moran and Flanagan resulted in a grand try by the last-named, Jolley failing with the gor.l kick. McDonald was ordered off for rough tackling, and the concluding stages were keenly contested. Result :—Wigan,4 goals 3 tries (17 points) ; Runcorn 1 goal 3 tries (11 points).

div.head: BARRY v. WIDNES.
div.p: BARRY v. WIDNES.

At Barry, before 2,000 spectators. Evans scored for Widnes in the first five minutes, but Davies failed. Dow scored it penalty goal for Barry, and O'Garry got over for the visitors. In the second half Power obtained a try for Barry, and Chick follow suit, the latter being converted._ Dow also landed a penalty goal, And Barry won a good game by 3 goals, 2 tries (12 points) to 2 tries (6 points.)

div.head: SHROVE TUESDAY MATCHES.
div.p: SHROVE TUESDAY MATCHES.
:Warrington at Halifax.

On Tuesday Warrington bad another stiff engagement at Halifax, and fared little better than at Oldham. Taylor and Dowell were absentees, but the side was in other respects a good OTIO. Beautiful weather again prevailed, and the day being a holiday at Halifax, a crowd of 9,000 people made their way to the Hanson lane ground. Halifax were at full strength, the team turning out\ as follows : _ _ _

Halitax—Little, back; Williams, Ward, and Dai Thomas, three-quarter_baoks ; Langhorn, Hammond, Morley, Mallinson, Robinson and Svvinhank, forwards. Warrington—Tilley, beck; Fish, Dickenson, Hocken- hall, and Treharne, three-quarter backs; Brooks and Jenkins, balf•backs ' • Boardman, O'Neill, Thomas, Belton, Chesters and Shuairs, forwards. Referee, Mr. F. Kennedy, Broughton. Totrzh judges, Messrs. H. Sewell, Leeds, and Shaw, Batley. Little started the game for Halifax, who soon becaras dangerous. Tiller defended well, but ultimately War- rington Were penalised, and Wedgwood kicked a goal The visitors continued to defend, and after Hockenhall had misflelded the ball, Doi Thomas got possession and scored behind the uprights, Wedgwood kicking a goal. Fish was profiainent in the succeeding play, and Halifax were driven to within a few yards of their line. Brooks kicked across towarda Treharne, hut Dai Thomas made, mark, and obtained relief. Warrington returned to the attack, and Fish had an unsuccessful shot at goal. Halifax then went with a rush to the other end, and Hilton nearly dropped a goal. Joe Riley soon after- wards received the ball from Hilton and scored a try which Wedgwood converted. Halifax kept up the attack, a round of passing by Hilton, Ward and Wedg- wood ending in Dai Thomas getting over at the pavilion corner after a fine sprint. Little failed at goal. The subsequent play was in favour of Warrington, a capital run by Fish being followed by clever combined play by Jenkins, Brooks, and Dickenson. Half-time—Halifax 3 goals and 3 tries (15 points), Warrington nil. In the beginning of. the second half play was fairly even for a time. Halifay then gained ground by pass- ing, but Ward, after making a good Opening, gave a bad pass to Williams. Hilton was soon afterwards injured, and took no further part in the game. Williams filled the vacancy at half back, and H. Morley was withdraw from the pack to the thren-quarter line.
SIZZSE=i

Halifax kept the upper band, and Williams scored a smart try, which Wedgwood failed to convert. War- rington next mode great headway, and the ball passed through the bands of Brooks and Jenkins to Dickenson, who cleverly beat the opposition and scored. G. Thomas failed at goal. Swinbank later scored for Hslifax, and Dai Thomas kicked a goal. In the final stages of the game Fish and Trebarne made several fine runs for Warrington, and Boardman scored a try, which Fish converted. Score :—Halifax 4 goals and 5 tries (23 points), Warrington 1 goal and 2 tries (8 points).

div.head: ROCHDALE HORNETS v. RUNCORN.
div.p: ROCHDALE HORNETS v. RUNCORN.

Four thousand .spectators witnessed this match t Rochdale on Tuesday afternoon. Both teams had absentees. The Hornets attacked vigorously, and Farrar dropped a splendid goal. West got over at the corner, after charging down a kick by one of the visitors .but be had been in touch, and the point was disallowed. Then Ledgard got possession, and dropped a neat goal. Runcorn raced sway, and Unsworth for Runcorn, and Ledgard for Rochdale missed glorious chances of scoring. Half-tilne—Rochdale Hornets 4 points, Runcorn nil. Soon after the resumption West scored for the Hornets after good play by Robinson and Schofield, and Baxter kicked a grand goal. Then West again dashed for the corner, but was tackled, and gas() to Robinson, who scored ehe second try. Baxter hitting the cross-barr with his shot at goal. West lost a fine opening later on •by heOtating, and Farrar made a magnificent save when faced with a couple of Runcorn men in possession of the ball. In the closing stages, Runcorn attacked, and scored an unconverted try from a forward rush. Result :—Rochdale Hornets, 3 goals 2 tries (12 points) ; Runcorn, 1 try (3 points.)

WARRINGTON ALBION V. SUTTON COMMERCIAL.— Great interest ctntred in the meeting of these teams on Walker's Drowery club ground on Saturday and expectations of a keen game were fully realized. Both sides had strong teams. Gillibrand started for the Albion, and Sutton at once went away, testing Monks in the first minute. Pendlebury now made a nice run for the Albion, but offside play spoiled their chances. Eventually Sutton took up the running, and nice com- bination ended in the centre opening the scoring. Silver-street entertained Heathside, and suffered defeat by five goals to four. The game was keenly contested, with Heathside always a shade better than their opponents. At times the winners' forwards were lamentably weak. Callan again was in form for the losers.

Beamont gave Parochial a severe fright, playing them to a draw. It was only in the last three minutes that the Parochial boys' drew level, Beamont having led 1-0 for three-parts of the game. The Trinity forwards, though hard ,working, could find no opening through the defence set up by Trantum and Dickenson. -
A keen game was seen between Arpley-street and St. Barnabas', the latter winning by the only goal scored.

div.head: ALLEGED SUSPICIOUS DEATH OF A CHILD
div.p: ALLEGED SUSPICIOUS DEATH OF A CHILD

At the Borough Police Buildings on Monday, Mr. Coroner Brighouse opened an inquiry into the circum- stances attending the death of Bertie Betley, son of Beatrice Betley, aged 19, a single woman of 14, Parr- street, Warrington. The child was born on Tuesday last and died two days later. The coroner addressing the jury, said that he was only going to take evidence of identification that morning, and that the inquiry would be adjourned until the 16th of next month. The case was a very serious one and would require very careful attention. The vital point of the crvo was for them to find out whether the child was illegally done to death or whether it died by accident. At one o'clock on Thursday last Dr. Manson (to whom much ctedit was due) gave information to the police regarding the case, and the at once made inquiries. It appeared that the mother of the child aged 19, who was employed up to last Monday as a seed warehouse hand. On the following day she complainad of being ill and while her mother (Mary Ellen Betley) was outside making a purchase, the child was born. On her return, at her daughter's request she went into a front room and saw the baby lying on the hearth stone with its head in contact with the fender. It was also covered up with a black skirt. A midwife was at once summoned and while she was handling the child it began to cry. The motber then said "put your hand over its mouth and stop it from crying. If my father bears it he will kill me." The child was carefully attended by the midwife, and Dr. Manson was called but despite all efforts, it died. On examination of the body, the right eye of the infant was found to be severely injured, and was very much swollen. There were also four or five scratch wound son the breast.

Mary Ellen Betley, grandmother of the child, who said she lived at 44, Parr-street, gave evidence of identification. The Coroner (to witness): I advise you and your daughter to be legally represented when the case again comes up for hearing, as a post mortem has bEen made on the body. It is a very serious case. and it has been suggested that the child has been illegally done to death. The inquiry was then adjourned until March 16th.

div.head: COMPULSORY 5111.1TrY TRAINING.
div.p: COMPULSORY 5111.1TrY TRAINING.
ARTICLE III: " The future is with the arbitrator and not with the warrior."

-Fortnnately provisions are within our reach, if we care to make use .of them, wheee,hy intern tional dis- putes can be settled without reserting to force. Amon, these provisions one is well worthy of mention. I now refer to the principle of pollination. The success of this great principle of mediation, especially during these latter years, affords considerable encouragement for the future. It is indeed, most surprising that vast numbers of men still look upon this plan as purely modern. But The principle has been doing ita beneficent work for many, rawly years ; and what it has been capable of achieving in the past is a source of much encouragement for its successful operation in the future. Amid the clement- for more armaments _ conseripoortist arely tne .re,W,l- - and equity of this principle, are gradually becoming manifest. It haS already ceminended itself to responsible Statesmen throughout the world aid there is every reason to believe there are yet greater-victories awaiting it. The morning trembles o'er the sky, And, unperceived, unfolds the spreading day. The future is ours. Whilst it is only too probable for some time that in times of popular passion the old barbaric method will be resorted to, yet men are coining more and more to see that war is too brutal and clumsy and .inherently incapable of equitably settling a quarrel. The victory lies with the biggest and best managed battalion, irrespective of equity and justice. Arbitration is consistent with fair play, reason and impartiality. Wild and unbridled passion plays no part in its decisions. It is an axiom that no man is a competent judge in his own cause. Arbitration possesses ethical standards but war knows none. Con- trast the respective effects of war and arbitration—and this comparison can be best made by utilising concrete examples. What results were prodneed by the Franco-G-erman War? Why, racial hatred, intense bitterness and rancour Even to this day the wounds have not healed. But what followed the Geneva Arbitration of 1871 in relation to the "Alabama " dispute? Were the after-effects similar to those in the former case? No ! Instead of national hatred there began almost imperceptibly a spirit of fellow- ship growing up between the U.S.A. and ourselves, and except for the dispute over the Venezuelan ques- tion, our relations since -that time have been most cordial. Surely this method is in keeping with the better spirit of the times. As far as individuals are concerned our case has been won. Why, the existence of our magistracy is a signal proof of the success of this same principle in relation to individual con- duct Oar Courts of Law are perMatiently established for the just settlement of individual differences. If Henry and George quarrel, and George immediately pounces upon Henry, would not the friends of George deem his conduct "ungentlemanly," to say the least of it? Then if it be ungentlemanly, even to use a polite phrase, for men to fight over their individual differences, surely this holds true when applied to nations. More so, to my mind, because the men who fight when the rulers of the nation disagree, are not the men who have ouarelled. When negotiations have ceased and con- flict ensues, it is not usual to find these rulers "at the front." In the old days, the King with his nobles, led the army ,into battle but now, the rulers generally stay at home and send Tommy Atkins to settle the matter. The whole thing is ludicious, outrageous and criminal. Just as nations have established courts cf justice within their own borders,so they should agree to create a great ,Permanent Court of Arbitration where all differences between themselves should be referred, for an impartial tribunal to settle. The nations have shown themselves capable of meeting each other on high and lofty ground. Ido not wish to ignore the complexity of the problems of Inter- nationalising. The whole subject is yet hazy and vague, ' which is only what one can reasonably expect. Chaos, more than order, characterise§ the situation. Interna- tional law is still in its infancy. But out of this chaos there is evolving an order which points the way to human progress. Mankind is aradually but surely, being re-shaped into something better and higher. Science, Art, Music and Literature etc., are playing a great part in this beneficent process. In the world of Science," Nationality," in the strict sense of the term plays no part. In Art, Music and Literature, there are no sharp lines of demarcation. Englishmen never dream of keeping the riches of Shakespeare to them- selves. His -writings are said to be more popular in Germany than in his own country. The masterpieces of 'Michael Angelo and Raphael can be as truly appre- dated by men who are not Italians, as the Italians themselves. And the popularity of Flanders " Messiah" among our own people these last few, years, is another proof of the glowing tribute of praise which one nation can best av on the son of another nation. Do not these things reveal to us the deeper and truer ties between nations, and men wh can thus fraternise, should be incapable of reserting to arms. Commerce is no longer confined within the borders of any one country. It is essentially cosmonelitan and exchange of nroduCts means exchange of services, and is it not a business truism that customers readily become friends ! Mutual goodwill is the fundamental condition of true progress and all these things provide striking evidence of the material, intelleetual. and mur.d solidnoity of mankind. In the presence of these great truths, arbitration should be the only natural method in settling the differences between peoples. Side by side with the idea of arbitration, another pacific idea already powerful is pressing forward, and growil3 into an International Law, namely the Law of mutrality. Whether nations will conscientiously observe these principles, is. a question usually asked. If we may take the past as a means of judging, there is every reason to believe that a jut and honourable'obedience will be forthcoming. Let us glance briefly at another phase of the relations between modern peoples. The co-ordinating and civilising influence of federation gives us an important clue to a way out' of present difficulties. I am not foolish enough to imagine that Europe can be federated yet, but there are already, indications that such a consummation is quite possible. It is many years since Carlyle wrote :—" The most cheering is this one thing, which we do see and know that the tendency is to a universal European commonweal that the wisest in all nations will communicate and co-operate, where Europe will again have its true Sacred College and Council of Amphictyons wars will become rarer, less inhuman, and in the course of centuries such delirious ferocity in nations, as in individuals it already is, may be proscribed and become obsolete for ever." This subject of federation is growingly important and in view of its inestimable value, I may, perhaps, be pardoned if I quote at length some words from Napoleon. Speaking at St. Helena of the Peace of Amiens, he said, "I had a project for general peace by drawing all the Powers to an immense reduc- tion of their standing armies. And then, perhaps, as intelligence became universally diffused, one might be permitted to dream of the application to .the great

Mr. 'TriEVELYA'II, who was very heartily received, said he had not come as a Minister to give them instructioos but, its a.privatei person to give thorn a few of his impressions. He was not quite certain that all Trunid Ditugerhur pleasing, but to put himself right with the teachers he would like to say that he most truly thought that their profession was to-day not only the most honourable but was ' very much the most powerful in England. The great army of teachers in this country was a product °Me last thirty years and by its coining the balance of moral influence had passed, for good or evil, from the philanthropist and the religious organization to the teacher and the schools. The making of the nation depended far more upon them than upon any other class in the community. What struck him most about the ordinary opinion with regard to our education system to-day in England was that the country was by no means in a state of Chinese satisfaction with its results. It was becoming more and more evident that we were only just beginning to understand the problems that we had got to solve. The country at large had ceased to be happy and contented in the conviction that the more money it spent and the more learned we should be, and was rather critically asking what were the products of the system. That feeling was summarised in the majority report of the Royal Commission on the Poor Law which suggested a thorough reconstruction of the time table and curriculum in order to supply a more suitable class of instruction and training for industrial pursuits. The ineffectiveness of our education moi.s, of course, due in many instances to purely social and economic reasons which were outside their control as educe. tionalists, though as citizens in other capacities they might have opportunities of remedying them.ln the case of the majority of childron,however,right schooling gave them a good chance of being right men. The great problem was to make our education not a temporary veneer but a permanent reality, a vital part in the life of every child, not easily forgotten as it often was now, that the child should look upon the school not as an imprisonment during eight years—and a rather less exciting and more boring imprisonment sometimes than the subsequent confinement in the factory—but enjoy it in the same kind of spirit that the properly taught child enjoyed play. It was a pity that the school -did not offer suffi- cient brightness and attraction to make the children,— whatever the motives of the parents might be—prefer the school to the mill. (A voice: "They do.") Well, the evidence was rather the other way. His idea was that children ought to feel an active and conscious pride in their schools, leave them with regret, and return to them with a, glad memory, and we were a long way from that now. (Hear, hear.) The

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, February 27, 1909.

European family of an institution like the American Congress or that of the Amphictyon in Greece, and I then what a perspective before us of greatness, of happiness of prosperity what a grand and magnificent; spectacle. However that may be, this agglomerationl of European peoples must arrive, sooner or later, byl the mere force of events. The impulse is already given, and • I do not think, after my fall, and the disappearance of my system, that any balance of power will be possible in Europe but this union and federation of the great nations.' 1 These prophetic utterances so identical in outlook have to some little extent been carried into practical effect. The most remarkable thing of the Hague Conferences, was not so much in what they did, or I did not accomplish, but that such gatherings had been possible. Here was the true greatness of the assembly land here was the germ of a world legislature. But prior to the year of 1899 -the year in which tbe first ' Conference was held - there had been continually ' growing for some time, a movement, thoroughly inter- national in scope and sympathy known as "The Postal Union." This Union practically comprises all the civilised nations of the world, whose governments are officially represented on the executive and possesses a permanent paid secretary who sits at Berne. The objects of this Union are to secure better and cheaper means of transit the wide world o'er, for letters and packages, etc Here again,is a movement, although rarely talked about, that is a forerunner of similar institutions which will gradually usher in a new are for mankind.

Just as Modern England is the fusion of the Ancient Heptarchy; and Great Britain the product of the four nationalities who hitherto had been at variance with each other at intermittent periods ; and the U.S.A. the union of the Federal States ; so Europe may yet become federated by the union of those great nati ms, who at present are foolishly piling up armaments against each other. The nations could then content themselves with a common organisation for the main- tenance of civil order. This is the sublimer policy for the time to come. As Kant exclaims : 'The world in becoming enlightened rises to unity." The time may not yet have arrived for the converting of swords into ploughshares, and spears into pruning hooks, but the advance of knowledge and civilisation foreshadows the-e.irnate disappearance of war." The National Service League would keep alive this spirit of separatism and in so doing be a stumbling block to these desirable =summations. , These things shall be A loftler race . Than e'er the world has known shall rise, With flame of freedom in their souls And light of knowledge 5n their eyes. Nation with nation, land with land, Unarmed shall live as comrades free ; In every heart and brain shall throb The pulse of one fraternity. Warrington.
H. GRAY.

high art of education was to get the child to find out things for himself and not to force him to accept what he was told. lie confessed he would like to sea in our schools more freetom on the part of the children to teach themselves, less of the lecture system of teaching, more encouragement to inquisitiveness and working by themselves on the part •of the children. In many schools he was not impressed by the kind of lessons he heard constantly being given, in which the teacher talked very nearly the whole time, and thought be had done well if he filled an hour in vigorous explaining. (LattAhter.) Our teachers were improving, but there was a great deal too much of the lecture system still in existence in our elementary and secondary schools. What we wanted to do was to get the teacher to under- stand that his main and even his sole duty was to get the child to work and think for itself. He would, rather sea a little less good spelling and a few snore intelligent sentences written by the children. He thought tintt after the very first stage the children should practically write nothing except accounts of things they cared about. Then it would be found that they would very soon care about writing and learn to write good English, and the spelling would very soon come by itself. (Laughter.) "You laugh at that" continued Mr. Trevelyan. "You have got to look over their shoulders, and to correct their spelling, but if you interest a child in its work the great •secret of teaching is that it will get over all these technical difficulties for itself if only you can interest it." (Applause). In an ideal system the teacher should not be the crammer of the child but the watcherand the maker of suggestions. To create a keen interest in school work and to make the child eojoy its work was to be a%first class teacher. We had abandoned largely the system of examinations —of which he personally was not such a violent oppon- ent as so'rne people—and the 'difficulty was to find a substitute—get the masses of these children to love their work, so that they would work as if something really depended upon it. He was afraid of a re-action against education not only on the ground of economy, but because it was possible the business classes of the country might turn round and say" What. is the good of all this elaborate training, if we cannot get people who can woick. Let us insist upon having in our schools some narrow technical training given to the children which shall fit them for this, that or the other trade ; or if you Am% give us that, give us the children earlier out of the schools in order that they may get a technical training." We had to set against suggestions like that the certainty that the children would go out from the schools thoroughly trained in band and mind. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN observed that the solution of the problem mentioned by /11r. tr' evelyan lay more with the .conditions under which the schools were managed than it did with the teachers. In Lancashire he believed there was a genuine affection on the part of children for their schools. Mr. A. 3. 301,LE7 said be was afraid that in War- rington the educational ladder was not yet a very high or a very wide one. In that respect the Town Council had not ennoaraged as it ought to have done the necessary expenditure which must be incurred if we were to have a real and not a sham educational ladder.
The MAYOR (Alderman Forshaw) then proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Trevelyan for his very able address.

Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P. seconded, and said: We give Mr. Trevelyan a hearty vote of thanks for paying us a visit in Warrington and our welcome to him is none the less cordial because he represents in Some measure ~the hereditary principle in politics and public service. His father Sir George Trevelyan will always be remembered both for his ability as a statesman and his grail literary distinction. Well, this literary and political distinction has been inherited by our friend Mr. Trevelyan and his distinguished brother, who is as you may remember, the biographer of Garibaldi. UT venture to say a word about education in the presence of such a gathering as we have hero to-night it would only be a suggestion or two which before so many experts on the subject I offer with deference and respect. It has always seemed to me that the best stjetultis to education from the earliest to the latest stages cf it is interest; the kind of interest in a subject whicb arouses curiosity in the best sense of the word, and touches the imagjaation. Bnt I know that there are many people who think that not only for boys and girls but for young men and women as well, a certain amount of compulsion in the matter of educa- tion would be a very good thing. I am not myself one of those who, so far at any rate' believe that in military matters a compulsory system is best suited to the needs of our nation. But that opinion does not blind me to the strength of some of the arguments used by those who approve of a compulsory system. Certainly it strotg argument is this, that ouch compulsion would be a stimulus to education in the ranks of the well-to-do classes. I was talking about this only this week to a Professor in London who has done a deal of teaching in his time. He said "Nonsense, there is a deal of exaggeration about education. Not one in twenty of you is worth it." I have since been wonder- ing whether my friend the Professor was referring to the nation—(laughter)—or the House of Commons when he said that. (Laughter.) His argu- ment was that the one man or woman in twenty would get for himself or herself all the education they needed fast enough. I won't quote him any further because I have too ranch respect for the feelings of my friends Canon Steveqson and Mr. Upson, and I do not want to see their hair tutn grey on the spot. (Laughter.) We know there are people of minus and extreme views on this and other queations, and there are some who even go further and say" Enough of literature ; perish the Press," and sigh for the times "When mankind shall be delivered from the clash of magazines, And the inkstand shall be shivered into thousand' smithereens, There shall stand a muzzled stripling, side by side a muzzled bore, When the Rudyards cease from Kipling, and the Haggards ride no more."—(Laughter). We can afford to smile at that kind of thing. And while none of us are in danger of forgetting for a moment the value of education in these days, we are equally alive to the still greater and even higher claims which it ever has upon us. After a reply from Mr. Trevelyan. and short speeches from Messrs. Storey (Manchester), Fletcher (Urmston) and Walker (Bolton), the meeting concluder/ with a vote of thanks to the Chairman, proposed by Councillor FULTON-SMITH, seconded by dr. W. H. STANSFIHLD.

div.head: MR. C. P. TREVELYATS Vißf. -- Criticisms of our Educational Methods.
div.p: MR. C. P. TREVELYATS Vißf. -- Criticisms of our Educational Methods.

Mr. C. P. Trevelyan, M.P., Parliamentary Secretary to the Board of Education, MIS the principal speaker at a public meeting on education held in the Parr Hall last evening under the auspices of the Lancashire County Ass)ciation of the National Union of Teachers. There was a fair. attendance, the audience consisting largely of members of the teaching profession. The Rev. Canon Morley Stevengort__presided and was sup- ported on the platform by NIG C.?. -TrevelYn Mr. A. H. Crosfield, ILP., the Mayor (Alderman Forshaw), Councillor Fulton-Smith (chairman or the Education Committee), Alderman Bennett, Councillors Birtles and Hawthorn, Rev. Father cN,ilson,,Messrs. C. E. Parker, A. J. Jolley, • E. Kin.dort E Plinston, J. Upson, J. Moore Murray (director of education), and other prominent educationists. • THE CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH. •

EDUCATION AND POLITICAL CONTROVERSY. The CIitaIRMAN said he oonsidered it a great honour and privilege to be allowed to preside over that meet- ing. Having spent the greater part of his life in work- ing for teachers and having made many friendships amongst them, he naturally felt the greatest possible sympathy for all that conceined the teaching profession and the welfare of its members. He was glad to know that that gathering was not political, although they welcomed most heartily a distinguished politician as their principal speaker, and to think that they would keep the controversial side of the education question out of their deliberations that evening. He could only wish that the time might not be long distant when the education question, hating been settled upon just and ecpitable lines, would be lifted once and for all out of the region of political controversy. The success which was attending and, they hoped, would continue to attenl Haldane's scheme for the Army was largely due to the fact that men of all shades of opinion had sank their politics in their patriotism and had worked together for the success of the scheme. Surely it VMS to the advantage of the nation that they should ho able to lift out of the realm of controversy these great national matters which affected us all so deeply. The politicians need not fear that they would have to join the ranks of the unemployed. (Laughter.) There would always be plenty of work for them to do and plenty of matters about which people would differ, but they as teachers would like to claim for education a place out out of the region of party strife in which all people might unite together to do what was best for the up-bringing of the future generation. There were many questions which they wished to discuss and many prOlems which they wished to solve. The age at which children should leave school, the size of their classes, the qualifications of their teachers,—these and such as these were the points which touched them as teachers and which they wished to settle upon the best lines. (Applause).

div.head: FIRE AT LONGFORD GAS WORKS.
div.p: FIRE AT LONGFORD GAS WORKS.

At about one o'clock yesterday afternoon a fire broke out at the Corporation Gas Works at Longford and the dense volumes of smoke emitted cast quite a pall over that quarter of the town. It appears that some grass in the works yard caught fire and a spark flew on to a heap of bags of creosote salts or napthaline, which is used to make fire lighters. The stack was soon a mass of flame. An army of workmen with barrels of soil and sand soon set to work to check the fire. In the meantime the Borough Fire Brigade was sent for and arrived on the scene under - the direction of Surperintendent Turner and his son the deputy superintendent, with the engine" Captain." Three or four hydrants were quickly got to work and the engine wat not required. Superintendent Turner met with an accident for as he was crossing from one side of the yard to the other, he slipped on a piece of timber and some of the burning material splashed in his eye. He at once received attention at the office and although he suffered great pain, he fortunately escaped any serious injury. By half-past two the flames were practically extinguished and as none of the bnildings were effected, the damage is comparatively slight.

div.head: Relief of the Distressed.
div.p: The Relief of the Distressed.

The distress in the to•A n through lack of employment still continues. The building trade which is generally in a prosperous condition at this time of the year remains dull, and shows little or no signs of improve- ment in the near future. The iron trade, to which the majority of persons being assisted through the agency of the Mayor's Fund belong, still remains quiet, and no immediate change seems probable. Much short time is being worked, many men with wives and families only being able to earn about ss. to 10s. a week, whilst others are unable to gaLemployment of any kind. Since the Mayor's Fund was opened 347 families have have been provided with food L'ic. At the present time there are the names of 200 families on the register who are being helped weekly, and over £l5O has already been spent. The Fund will very soon be exhausted unless fresh subscriptions are forthcoming.

div.head: TEACHERS' CONFERENCE.
div.p: TEACHERS' CONFERENCE.
the Lancashire Association.

To-day (Saturday) the annual meeting of the Representative Assembly of the Lancashire County Association (National Union of Teachers) will be held in the Wycliffe Hall, Warrington. Tbis is the first time that the conference has met in Warrington and considerable interest is being taken in . the event by the local members of the profession. Ab,ut 200 delegates from all parts of Lancashire, representing 9,000 members are expected to attend. The Lancashire Association is the largett county organization of teachers in the country. The morning will be devoted to various sectional gatherings and, at 2.30 in the afternoon the general meeting will be held. It will be a matter of gratification to the teachers of Warring ton and the townspeople generally that Mr. John Upson to be elected to the presidency. He succeeds Mr. W. Carr, of Morecambe, in that high office. Mr. Upson is a very highly respected member of the profession and has spared no effoit to advance the interests of teachers. Such is the confidence reposed in him that he has twice been elected president of the Warrington branch of the N.U.T. and he acted as secretary for six yews and treasurer for eight years. He has repre- sented the teachers on the Warrington Education Committee for the past , six years and he has been a delegate to no fewer than ten annual conferences. On being installed president of the Lancashire Association this afternoon, Mr. Upson will deliver an interesting address on educa- tional topics. (-;

Hope soon died from Warrington breasts at Oldham. Five hundred people followed the Warrington team full (4 confidence in their ability to give a .good account of themselves and perhaps break Oldham's inviolable home record. The prevailing opinion even at Oldham was that the home side would have all their work cut out to win. Warrington's prowess was fully recognised, but 'unfortunately it was not demonstrated during the play. Watersheddings was ever a bad ground for Warrington, and the result was according to tradition. Oldham won easily by 18 points, and at one time they looked like wiping out the 27 —nil defeat sustained at Warrington. It was the dearest wish of the Oldhamer's heart to be revenged on the Wirepullers for that humiliating blow three months ago, and nearly 25,000 people assembled to witness the deed.
With the conditions ideal Warrington should have done well, but they shaped very poorly and could

hardly be recognised as the same side which has performed such brilliant scoring feats of late. Over-eagerness may have had something to do with the failure of the backs, for it was plain to see that they wore keen enough The chief 'cause of Mire was found in' the scrumonsa, however, for here. Warrington systematically played second fiddle and did not get the ball more than once iu lour " tussles. Naturally, the halves had a very trying time .and got few opportunities of making openings for the men behind. Seeing that the- Warring- ton six played a brilliant game in the open, and twice came within inches of scoring, it is pretty obvious that there must have been some shirking in the pack. Oldham have suffered from the same fault in recent matches, but on Saturday the men put their heads down with a will and destroyed the other side's plan of campaign in the way vigorous, determined for- ward play always will.

There was another factor which contributed to Warrington's undoing. In the early stages of the game, Beynon persistently persevered with short kicks from the scrum along the gronnd. This is foreign to Oldham's tactics, but the plan had the effect of spoiling the nerve of the Warrington halves and centres. They were continually running back to save, and frequently found themselves out of position. In fact the rear division seen:red demoralised when Arthur Smith the International forward, got hold and rushed clean through with the first try. After this the Oldham men played a more orthodox game, though their combination was never high-class and much of the passing went straight across the field. Tyson got a good try after Smith had taken him down to Fish, but the concluding 8 points were the result of . flaky chances snapped up by men playing with the utmost confidence. Smith was the best of the home team's back division and showed that he is still a great three- quarter.

Apart from the weakness in the serum. Warrington were badly handicapped by the absence of Taylor. Hockenhall played like a man out of practice —could one expect more —and Treharne seemed to be quite demoral- sed. He made more blunders on Saturday than he has done all the time he has woin the Warrington colours. iDickenson and Fish did a lot of work on the defence, but the wing man never once got a decant pass. Not much can be said for the halves, who might have done much better with even the few opportunities they had. Until the last ten minutes Brooks was as erratic as he knows how to be. He made only one break away throughout the game, and it was in the very last moment of the match. Neither of them tackled Avery in anything like an effective fashion. Warrington were well-beaten and deserved to be. That ends it !

It was a severe ordeal for Warrington to meet two of the League leaders on their own grounds in succes- sive matches, for the home clubs could not afford to drop a point and thus played for all they were worth. The Wirepullers were at Halifax on Tuesday, and fared little better than at Oldham, though they played a better game. Halifax were stronger, faster, and more determined, and to ok full advantage of Warring- ton's weakness on the right wing. It was only in the second half that Warrington got into their stride, an d the home team i were then 15 points ahead. Warrington quickly put on 8 points, and Halifax another 8, the final score being 23-8. . . .

The best men on the Warrington side were Fish and Dickenson. who both played a fine game. Fish made some brilliant runs, and on one occasion cross- kicked to such effect that the forwards had a walk- over, but. Boardman knocked-on. Brooks again played a long way below form, and practically gave two tries away through ldsing possession at a critical moment. It is to be hoped he recovers his skill and nerve for to-day's enconnter. At one time G. Thomas was absent for a quarter of an hour through injury, and near the close Hilton of Halifax got heavily tackled near the line and was carried off in great pain. Fortunately he recovered afterwards and the injury is not likely to prove serious.

div.head: Col. Hugh Whatmore's Visit.
div.p: Col. Hugh Whatmore's Visit.

To-morrow (Sunday) .will be a great day in the history of the Warrington Corps of the Salvation Army, as Colonel Hugh Whitmore, 'Field Secretary of Great Britain, will visit the town accompanied by Brigadier George Holmes and others. Colonel W hatmore has had charge of Salvation Army work in various countries, and can speak seven different languages. the morning at 11 o'clock a holiness convention will be held in the Salvation Army Hall, Academy-street. At 2 p.m. there will be a great Rally at the top of Winwiek-street. All the various temperance organisations will be ,met and will then march to the Parr Hall, where 'at" 3 p.m. Colonel Whatmore will lecture on " Drink and its evils." At 6.45 the Colonel will conduct a great Salvation meeting in the Parr Hall.

CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIP. Warrinfrton to tin Fora. The 27th annual cross-country championships of the Northern Counties WilS decided on Saturday last, on the Doncaster Race C3urse, and not at Haydock Park, the scene of the contests fur the last eight years. There was a record entry of 53 clubs, 15 senior and 43 junior. There were several thousand spectaturs. THS JUNIOR R1C1.3.-A WAR,RINGT3N CLU BS VICTORY , In the junior race, 208 runners started, representing 139 teams. Ryland's Workmen and Lineaster Friends were not represented. At two miles Warburton (Bury A.C.) led from Drink- water • (St. Helens), Vose (Warrington), . and Lord (Wibsey Park). When six miles had been covered, Warburton had increased his lead, being followed by Lord, with lin!se third. At the completion of the race (71 miles) Lord had reduced Warburton's lead, but the latter won comfortably by 200 yards, with Shaw (York Harriers). The winners' time was 43 rain. 8 sec. Hulse (Tally-ho) was fourth, H. Holbrook (Warrington A.C.) fifth, IL Jepson (Warrington A.C.) sixth, C. Vose (Warrington United) seventh,H. Herbert (Liverpool Boundary) eight, W. Antrobas (Warrington A.C.) ninth, and L. Drinkwater (St. Helens Recreation) tenth. Team placings ;—Warrington A.C., 109 points, 1 ; Wibsey Park, 121, 2 ; Sheffield United, 110, 3 ; Artuley and Wortley, 162, ' Warrington United, 161, 5 ; aed York Harriers, 231, 6. THE SENIOR RACE.-0. J. STRAW SECOND.
